#78. How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (662 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

How long can a 1000 watt-hour power station run your devices?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (662 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than you might expect.
  • This is anecdotal, perhaps, but based on the number of ads I'm bombarded with, it feels like portable power stations have become a hot commodity in the last several years.
  • A critical question to ask is how much power you actually need.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Determining the stamina of your portable power station is more complicated than you might expect.

This is anecdotal, perhaps, but based on the number of ads I'm bombarded with, it feels like portable power stations have become a hot commodity in the last several years. And it makes sense — in a society increasingly dependent on phones and laptops, not to mention other electronics, even the best small power banks just won't cut it during a prolonged outage. And of course, these stations have always had uses outside the home, such as camping or job sites.

A critical question to ask is how much power you actually need. More isn't always better, since a high-end station is not only expensive, but considerably larger and heavier. A multi-kilowatt station might cost as much or more than the devices it's powering and require help to lift if you've been neglecting the gym.

Let's take 1,000Wh (watt-hours) as a baseline. How long can you reasonably expect that to last when the power goes out at home or you're watching YouTube in the Adirondacks? The answer is surprisingly complicated. It depends on what you plug in, how it's actively operating, and how efficient your power station is at converting energy.

It has been revealed that while there are plenty of options out there from brands like Anker and EcoFlow, let's take the Jackery Explorer 1000 v2 as an example. It's rated at 1,024Wh, and can deliver up to 1,500W of output. Simple math suggests that a 200W fridge, for example, could run for over five hours, or that a 65W laptop could last for well over 15 hours.

In a recent development, in practice, however, even Jackery only promises four hours for that fridge and 11 hours for the laptop. So what gives? The answer is power conversion. When you plug into a station's AC outlet, that power has to be converted from DC, possibly wasting anywhere from 5 to 20 percent in the process. Total efficiency is impossible, and you might make things even less efficient if you plug in something like the wall adapter for your phone or tablet, which converts AC back to DC.

Industry observers note that it's also worth noting that the rated consumption for devices can vary wildly in practice. A gaming laptop might consume a few dozen watts when it's browsing the web, but well over 200W when it's running full tilt. Even your phone is going to have ebbs and flows, based on what it's trying to do — it takes a lot more more juice to stream a TV show over 5G than it does to add those crackers to your calorie counter.

In a recent development, for a start, if a station has built-in USB ports, plug your phones, tablets and other mobile devices into those whenever possible. You'll reduce the inefficiency created by plugging in adapters. Naturally, this also frees up AC outlets, allowing you to plug in other critical gear.

It has been revealed that pay attention to ambient temperatures, too. While something like the Jackery 1000 is rated for output at temperatures from 14 to 113F (-10 to 45C), the optimal range for its LiFePO4 (lithium iron phosphate) batteries is actually around 59 to 95F (15 to 35C). You'll get less power out a battery that's extremely cold or extremely hot, so simply keeping a station in the shade or properly ventilated could make a world of difference.

In the long term, consider the impact of charging cycles. There's a difference between battery capacity and battery life, and as with any rechargeable battery device, the usable capacity of your portable power station shrinks over time, based largely on how many full cycles (or their equivalent) you've gone through. It may be hard to put a dent in something with a kilowatt-level supply, but that should be a reason to avoid draining a power station unless you really need it.

#76. Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed

📅 13 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (600 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ars Technica ↗ Open Full Page

Millions of Americans are not taking their GLP-1 drugs as prescribed

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (600 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days.
  • Industry observers note that in a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025.
  • According to recent reports, among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that GLP-1 medications are everywhere these days. The peptide-based drugs are both highly effective and wildly popular for diabetes, weight loss and a growing range of connected chronic health conditions, including cardiovascular disease and obstructive sleep apnea. But, amid the boom, the latest data suggests millions of Americans have turned to unapproved versions and are using the potent drugs in ways doctors never intended, raising questions about what that real-world use means for safety and efficacy.

Industry observers note that in a study published this week, researchers at the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention broke down survey data of GLP-1 use collected between July and August of 2025. Based on responses from over 8,000 US adults, the researchers estimate that about one in 10 US adults (9.8 percent) used a glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist, aka GLP-1 medication, in 2025. That’s around 27 million adults. The study was published in the CDC’s Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report.

According to recent reports, among GLP-1 users, nearly half (44 percent) reported using their GLP-1 in a way that was different from how it was prescribed. Users skipped doses, delayed getting refills, and used smaller doses than prescribed, among other changes. More than half of the people modifying how they used the drug said the changes were because of cost or availability reasons. Cost and access barriers were most pronounced among younger GLP-1 users. Fifty-eight percent of adults 14­–39 years old who modified their use cited cost as a barrier, compared with just 20 percent of adults 65 or older who said the same.

In a recent development, modified use of GLP-1 medications was particularly common among those using compounded versions of GLP-1 medications. Among all GLP-1 customers, at least 23 percent used a compounded version; an additional 9 percent said they didn’t know whether their GLP-1 was compounded or not.

Recent findings suggest that these versions of GLP-1 drugs are made by compounding pharmacies and are intended to mimic a medication approved by the Food and Drug Administration, such as Wegovy or Ozempic. But compounded drugs themselves are not approved by the FDA; the regulatory agency does not review their safety, effectiveness, or quality before they’re sold. While compounded drugs are considered more accessible and affordable, they generally have higher rates of preparation errors, contamination, and other manufacturing problems compared to non-compounded drugs.

Sources indicate that among people who used these unapproved, potentially riskier GLP-1s, 62 percent were not taking them as prescribed. That’s compared to just 36 percent of GLP-1 users who took brand-name drugs.

In a recent development, the potential risks of taking unapproved GLP-1 drugs at all or taking them in unapproved ways may be missed by users, the CDC researchers note. A 2025 study assessing websites selling compounded GLP-1 medications found that nearly 40 percent of sites stated or implied the drugs were FDA-approved, making it harder for consumers to differentiate the compounded versions from FDA-approved ones. Further, nearly 80 percent of sites used brand names in their advertising, which could further mislead consumers. The researchers noted that using brand names violated FDA regulatory standards.

Recent findings suggest that “Given the substantial use of compounded GLP-1 medications, understanding the safety and quality of compounded GLP-1 medications is an notable public health consideration,” the authors conclude. They also call for more research on the common modifications people are using, such as dose and frequency adjustments, saying the data on the safety and effectiveness of these real-world practices “could help guide the development and implementation of clinical guidelines and support appropriate medication use.”.

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the organization’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

It has been revealed that the petition website stated the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

Huang resigned on Thursday, four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs.

Industry observers note that nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the organization’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding.

Why your Wi-Fi slows down when more devices connect

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (728 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.
  • According to recent reports, demands on home Wi-Fi have increased considerably over the past decade, never mind the launch of the first routers way back in the 1990s.
  • According to recent reports, that can create a real crunch on performance.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your Wi-Fi router is like a busy train station, and once you get a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep the incoming and outgoing traffic humming.

According to recent reports, demands on home Wi-Fi have increased considerably over the past decade, never mind the launch of the first routers way back in the 1990s. It used to be that homes had a handful of connected devices at most, typically massive-ticket items like PCs and game consoles. Today, there's a good chance your watch is online too, and that you've got a plethora of cool smart home gadgets ranging from lamps to smart speakers.

According to recent reports, that can create a real crunch on performance. But why is that, exactly? You probably know part of the answer, yet there may be more going on than you imagine. Your Wi-Fi router isn't just a series of tubes — a better analogy might be a central train station with complicated lines of incoming and outgoing traffic.

Once you have a sense of how things work, it's easier to keep this congestion under control. It's not just about minimizing the number of connected devices — controlling how and when gadgets connect can also have a substantial impact.

All Wi-Fi routers have an internal bandwidth cap, but there are some differences between types of home internet. Wi-Fi 6 and 6E routers top out at 9.6Gbps, whereas Wi-Fi 7 ups the ceiling to 46Gbps. Although you're unlikely to approach even the 9.6Gbps mark, which is well beyond the scope of most internet looks, we should emphasize that these limits represent total available bandwidth — going not just to and from the internet but locally between devices. If someone's transferring a few dozen gigabytes of video from their camera to their laptop, it could create momentary congestion if a bunch of other devices are also trying to run full-tilt.

In a recent development, complicating matters is the glitch of band congestion. Wi-Fi 6 provides 2.4 and 5GHz bands, while 6E and 7 add a 6GHz option. Each band is allocated only so many channels, so if a band fills up, the result is likely to be delays or a kick over to another band, assuming a device supports it and that your router isn't using separate band IDs. The 2.4GHz band is particularly easy to overwhelm, since there are only three non-overlapping channels, and many low-power accessories don't have 5 or 6GHz has a option.

In fact, all routers have an invisible limit on simultaneous connections, which is why you should upgrade immediately if you're still using Wi-Fi 5. That protocol may only be able to handle as few as 10 to 25 active devices, and it's going to boot older connections to make room for latest ones once that limit is reached. I learned this the hard way when I started reviewing smart home gear in the 2010s.

Upgrading to Wi-Fi 7 may help, but be warned that it's not a magic bullet. It's still possible for a band to become overloaded. To truly take advantage of Wi-Fi 7's features — such as "preamble puncturing," which allows a channel coping with interference to be carved out for its remaining bandwidth — both your router and connecting devices need to support it. Chances are, most of the devices you own are still limited to Wi-Fi 6 or 6E.

It has been revealed that with or without Wi-Fi 7, it may help to steer as many devices as possible over to 5 or 6GHz if your router allows the creation of separate band logins. It's a win-win. While those bands have shorter range than 2.4GHz, they offer both less congestion and faster connection speeds for the devices that support them.

That's not an option on mesh routers, however, so you may need to resort to other tactics, such as using your router's app controls to pause unnecessary devices when a particular upload or download is crucial. In the long term, you should consider migrating as many smart home accessories as possible over to hub-based setups, particularly light bulbs. While standalone Wi-Fi bulbs are cheap and easy to set up, each one has to compete for available channels. Conversely, a hub can link dozens of products via protocols like Thread or Zigbee while only demanding a single Wi-Fi connection.

According to recent reports, rachelle Hampton is a writer and co-owner at Defector Media, and the host of Normal Gossip, a podcast of anonymous listener-submitted stories about everyday drama. Whether that’s lies about luxury wool in a literal knitting circle, the impeachment of a hypocritical HOA president, or a COVID outbreak at a destination wedding with an absurd 25 bridesmaids, each story is unique in its absurdity, yet weirdly relatable.

Recent findings suggest that after years as one of the co-hosts of Slate’s In Case You Missed It, a podcast that required her to be chronically online, Hampton is enjoying being a little more unplugged these days. And she has perhaps the most interesting answer we’ve ever received to the question “what’s worth splurging on?”.

What is your most indispensable tool (analog or digital, app or hardware)?

According to recent reports, I think it has to be the Notes app. My entire life is in there! My relationship to the Notes app definitely changes depending on what’s going on in my life at the time. Sometimes I just use it to make my grocery lists, but there was also a period of time where I used it to house my weekly to-do list, so it was basically the only thing between me and destruction. I’ve started blog drafts in the Notes app, and I’ve used it to write out particularly fraught text messages. There are recipes I’ve developed in there, as well as passwords and also questions for my doctors. The first note in my phone is from 2018, so it also serves as a nearly decade-long journal, though there are definitely notes that I simply can’t decipher, like why do I have a note from July 2020 that just says “4th floor”?

Which is the most underappreciated?

Recent findings suggest that I absolutely hate texting. (I write all day, I don’t want to do it in my free time!!) But as someone who also refuses to delete their texts, I have to acknowledge that my most significant personal archive is probably in my Messages inbox.

What is the first app you install on a newly introduced phone or computer?

Industry observers note that it’s a tie between Spotify and whatever phone game I’m presently addicted to, which for the last two years has been Township. I’ve never played Sims or Animal Crossing, but I’m told that it’s something like that. I just like planting my little crops.

How many tabs do you have open right now?

I maintain inbox zero across my entire digital life, so I close all my tabs after I finish a task. Right now I have three tabs that I will close immediately after finishing this questionnaire: the first is the Google Doc I’m typing in, the second is the landing page for this series, and the third is a Google tab where I just searched Animal Crossing to make sure I had the name right.

Which social media platform do you use the most?

It’s a tie between Reddit and YouTube. Hosting a twice-weekly podcast about the internet for three years either gave me some sort of PTSD or cured me of my social media addiction, depending on how you want to look at it. I can’t spend more than twenty minutes max on IG or X or Bluesky without feeling claustrophobic. The exception is when I’m sick, and I let my fever brain rot on IG reels. Otherwise, it just feels like too much information from too many different sources. Reddit and YouTube are both places where I feel somewhat in control of what I’m seeing.

What is your happy place online?

I don’t think I’ve ever been as happy online as I was on Tumblr between 2013 and 2016. I’m always subconsciously chasing that high.

What is your favorite gadget you’ve ever owned?

Sources indicate that my older brother bought me a tabletop Klipsch Bluetooth speaker for Christmas a couple of years ago, and it’s still going strong. The sound quality is incredible, and the design is super sexy, so it doesn’t immediately read as a Bluetooth speaker, which I love. I hope I never have to replace it.

Which tech trend do you wish would go away?

In a recent development, one of the stances I’m proudest of is that I’ve never (intentionally) used ChatGPT or Midjourney or any of the other generative AI tools / large language models. It’s getting harder and harder to avoid now that Gemini is built into Google and its various products. Stop trying to write my emails, Gemini!! I’ve never been swayed away from my belief that every single AI firm owes a bankrupting amount of money to the writers and artists whose work their products are built on. Until that debt is paid, there’s nothing appealing to me about talking to a chatbot or creating a shitty poster.

What creation are you most proud of?

In 2020, when I was a staff writer at Slate, I spent a [redacted amount of time] methodically charting and ranking all 349 times Stephenie Meyer used the word murmur in her iconic Twilight saga. The idea had been germinating somewhere in the recesses of my brain for over a decade, only to be released by the surprise 2020 release of Midnight Sun. Seeing this blog come to life (shout out Slate’s interactive designer Natalie Matthews-Ramo!) felt like a fever dream come true.

What is your current obsession?

I’ve rewatched every episode of Netflix’s I Like to Watch with drag queens Trixie Mattel and Katya an embarrassing amount of times. There are certain episodes, like this one where Trixie and Katya react to Wake Up Dead Man: A Knives Out Mystery, that I can quote front to back.

What do you do when you’re feeling stuck?

Industry observers note that I wish I could say something chill and zen like take a cold shower or something, but the truth is when I’m writing and feeling stuck, I usually smoke a little weed, preferably a sativa strain. Getting high gets me out of my own way, which is usually the problem when I’m feeling stuck. It particularly helps with scriptwriting for Normal Gossip because the tone is so conversational, so being a little bit high stops me from over-writing.

When was the last time you went somewhere without your phone?

My favorite coffee shop is less than 500 ft from my apartment, so I end up there without my phone at least once a week, either on purpose or by accident.

What do you think is worth splurging on?

Butter! With the caveat that I live by myself and don’t bake, so butter lasts a while in my household, but good butter can change a whole meal. It makes eating toast feel like a luxury instead of a chore to be completed between meetings because I’ve forgotten to eat lunch. My floor for butter is Kerrygold, but recently I’ve been loving this French brand called Isigny Sainte-Mère.

What would the tagline for your biopic be?

Last to arrive, first to leave.

What’s the last GIF or meme you used?

A free daily digest of the news that matters most.

#70. Latest Update: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: It’s Getting Too Dry for Even Cactuses to Survive

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency.
  • Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections.
  • “The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The humble cactus is an icon of resiliency. Stuck in a desert with little rain and abundant searing sun, these plants don’t just survive, they thrive—and in turn provide habitat for owls and other birds, and flowers for bats and other pollinators.

Yet cacti are in serious trouble, due to habitat loss and the poaching of species for private collections. Now we can add worsening droughts to those woes, according to a new study in the journal Nature. Researchers modeled a future of not just relentlessly rising temperatures but also the attendant dry spells, finding that the majority of nearly 1,000 cactus species will lose habitat as the climate radically changes. More than a quarter of those species could lose at least 80 percent of that habitat by 2100.

“The public perception of cacti tends to be of these organisms that are extremely drought-adapted and are just resilient, can handle anything that you throw at them,” said Michiel Pillet, a conservation ecologist at the University of South Florida and lead author of the paper. “In reality, cacti are absolutely amazing—and they’re my favorite plant group, clearly—but they’re not that different from other plants.”.

That means cacti need water. In the deserts of the southwestern United States, for example, they rely on seasonal monsoon rains, which tend to make July or August the wettest month in a given year. Because this is still a desert, cacti have evolved a range of adaptations to survive, like a waxy skin that helps them retain that bounty of rainwater. “Just like other plants, they evolved under conditions that they’re used to,” Pillet mentioned. “When you take them outside of those conditions, they might not be able to handle that.”.

Think of these cacti like sick hospital patients. Someone might be admitted for heat-related illness, as their body struggles to cool itself. At the same time, though, they might be dehydrated. Cacti are dealing with the same stresses, as global temperatures rise and dry spells intensify. “When we consider drought conditions, then it turns out that they’re much, much sicker than we previously thought,” Pillet stated. “These results really do change the outlook of cacti, and most likely plants more broadly under climate change.”.

It has been revealed that instead of simply modeling these threats going forward, the researchers turned to the citizen science platform iNaturalist, where people upload photos of plants and animals. This provided 650,000 observations of cacti in the wild, helping paint a clearer picture of how species might be faring.

Sources indicate that really, this isn’t a simple matter of cacti withering and dying. Sure, if relentless droughts take hold, individuals can’t get water. But the stress could be temporally complex, too. “Now we can move towards questions of: What life stages are most affected?” Pillet said. “Is it the adults or is it the seedlings? But also, which processes? Is it reduced growth or is it increased mortality? Or are plants failing to flower?”.

Put another way: Cactus species could be suffering from sublethal effects of drought—the lack of water may not kill them immediately but still interfere with their reproduction. And without procreation, populations shrink. In the Sonoran Desert, for example, the iconic, towering saguaro is reproducing less frequently during prolonged droughts, because they’re not always flowering.

Part of the problem is that while desert ecosystems may look tough and hardened overall, they’re in fact quite fragile. “They don’t recover quickly once they are disturbed, or once they are degraded, just because there’s so little water and such higher temperatures,” mentioned Marcos Robles, the Nature Conservancy’s lead scientist in Arizona, who wasn’t involved in the research. “It takes multiple decades to recover, and in some cases, they don’t recover.”.

Now drought is compounding with other stressors, like habitat loss and poaching, to drive cactus species to the brink. On the opposite end of the spectrum, too much water from rising seas has led to the local extinction of the Key Largo tree cactus in Florida. Higher nighttime temperatures are a problem, too, since that’s when saguaro and other cacti respire to avoid water loss. “If the nighttime temperatures are very high, they can’t do it,” said Rod Haenni, president of the nonprofit Cactus and Succulent Society of America, who wasn’t involved in the paper. “Then if you water on top of that, the plants just rot.”.

Still, some cactus species may persist by picking up and leaving. Well, not individual plants, but populations could creep into areas with climates that more closely match what the species adapted to all those millennia ago. A similar thing is happening in the Arctic, actually, where some plants are marching farther north in “search” of increasingly agreeable weather and more water.

Industry observers note that in the end, the purpose of this sort of research is to better inform where conservation professionals might concentrate their efforts. They can’t stop droughts, of course, but they can evacuate enough cacti to establish populations in botanical gardens, where they can be cared for as the climate grows more unrecognizable to even the hardiest desert vegetation. Species can even be reintroduced to the wild in some cases, so long as drought and high temperatures don’t remain a threat to a population.

Governments, too, need to protect the lands where cacti are threatened, Haenni remarked. This new research, he added, could make that happen. “Hopefully, it’ll wake people up,” Haenni said. “But the problem is that a lot of the governments involved are indifferent to this. There are a lot of people in the countries who are not indifferent, but they’re not running the governments.”.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening.
  • “Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Duffy posted on X.
  • It has been revealed that over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Federal Administration lifted its third-ever nationwide ground stop after several hours Friday evening. Domestic flights were cleared to begin taking off at 8:35 pm EST. FAA Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy cautioned that, barring massive system updates, there will be “more of these” ahead.

“Today’s nationwide ground stop happened because our air traffic control system is operating on DECADES-OLD analog equipment that simply cannot compete with the demands of the 21st century,” Duffy posted on X.

It has been revealed that over a million travelers have been affected by the delays, with some airlines cancelling flights for the remainder of Friday. “Due to the ongoing ground stop, Air Canada has cancelled all flights to and from the United States for the remainder of the evening,” the airline noted.

The stoppage began at 3:36 pm EST Friday afternoon, days after expanding use of an AI tool, when the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop, halting departures from all US airports. Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy declared the ground stop on X, citing a “communication concern impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers.” Duffy promised updates as more information is known and said FAA staff was troubleshooting the problem.

In a recent development, department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said that the ground stop was not prompted by a security threat. “This is a telecommunications outage out of the FAA. Out of an abundance of caution, we have grounded all of the flights,” Mullin said. “There’s no indication as of yet that this is a nefarious attack against us.”.

Mullin had said the FAA would handle incoming international flights on a case-by-case basis.

Recent findings suggest that this was only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the FAA. The first, and most memorable, came during the attacks of September 11, 2001, when the FAA stopped all civilian departures nationwide and subsequently ordered all airborne aircraft to land. Commercial flights did not take off again until September 13. Flights were also grounded for less than two hours the morning of January 11, 2023, after its Notice to Air Missions system suffered an outage.

It has been revealed that unfortunately for travelers, it turned out to be a lengthy ground stop. Airlines were quick to cancel flights scheduled to leave later in the day, with American Airlines warning that disruptions were expected for the rest of the day.

Sources indicate that “This is going to take some time,” Mullin stated. “Flights are accounted for, and there should be no fear to the public at all.”.

This story was updated at 10:03 pm EST to report the ground stop was lifted.

#66. Where was Nvidia’s security team?

📖 Baca
Hardware & Chips ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 TechCrunch ↗ Open Full Page

Where was Nvidia’s security team?

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1097 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: TechCrunch

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August.
  • It has been revealed that at the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons.
  • In a recent development, reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, outsiders had little reason to notice when Nvidia’s longtime chief security officer and head of product security stepped down in August. Just two and a half months later, CEO Jensen Huang himself left the firm over growing questions about his extramarital relationships — starting with an executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore data center company that U.S. investigators suspect of funneling Nvidia chips to China, then widening to reports about two separate affairs with Nvidia employees.

It has been revealed that at the time, David Reber, who spent four years as CSO and seven at Nvidia overall, said he was leaving for health reasons. “This wasn’t a pivot I had planned. But I know what needs to come first: family and health,” he wrote on LinkedIn in late August, disclosing that he’d been diagnosed with young-onset Parkinson’s more than two years ago.

In a recent development, reber’s replacement, Saša Zdjelar, previously spent 17 years at ExxonMobil in Houston, leaving as a senior IT manager before spending one year at Salesforce and several years at the cybersecurity company ReversingLabs. Zdjelar didn’t respond to questions Thursday about the transition or what the security team knew.

Nothing public connects Reber’s or Zdjelar’s role changes to the Megaspeed matter, but it seems fair to wonder what Nvidia’s security team knew about the government’s scrutiny of Megaspeed and about Huang’s relationships, and whether anyone raised concerns. Reber didn’t respond to questions Thursday. Nvidia also has not answered our related questions.

Relationships between a CEO and his employees typically fall to HR, legal and the board, not security. But security specialists say any affair — even one inside the office — can give a foreign intelligence service leverage over an exec who wants it kept quiet.

Sources indicate that still, spotting the clues isn’t easy. The way intelligence services collect information, much of it through everyday conversation rather than hacking, makes it especially difficult for security teams to identify risks, according to retired senior intelligence officer Nicholas Eftimiades, who says he has trained more than 1,000 corporate security professionals.

Sources indicate that some people inside Nvidia clearly knew parts of the picture. Nvidia’s top lawyer was engaged with the government’s Megaspeed inquiry more than a year ago, The Latest York Times reported earlier this week. (Nvidia has said it regularly contacts officials.) Reports about Huang’s relationships with employees suggest colleagues also knew of them, even if the behavior is not expressly forbidden by Nvidia’s code of conduct. The Times cited five Nvidia employees who said he was involved with a vice president who reported directly to him; Reuters, citing two people, later reported a second relationship. What’s unclear is whether any of that reached security.

Even if it had, Eftimiades, who wrote Chinese Espionage Operations and Tactics in 2020, told TechCrunch that a security team’s resources are often limited. For one thing, they’re often underfunded because, unlike some other cost centers, they don’t drive revenue. It’s astonishingly common for CEOs to answer a security team’s warnings with “not a nickel more than compliance,” he remarked.

Many companies also define security overly narrowly, specialists say. In an opinion piece in The Hill, Don Aviv, CEO of the corporate investigations firm Interfor International, and author Jeremy Hurewitz, wrote, “Too many companies still approach security primarily as a matter of protecting facilities, preventing cyberattacks, and responding to physical threats.” The two argued that “[s]ecurity teams need to pay greater attention to insider threats, including the cultivation of executives and employees by foreign intelligence services, suspicious business relationships, conflicts of interest and attempts to obtain sensitive information through trusted personal contacts.”.

It would be surprising if Nvidia’s security team didn’t have a more expansive remit than most companies given its scale and business partners, but it’s possible.

In a recent development, in fairness, some of it is simply beyond what any team can do. Speaking generally, not about Huang, Eftimiades offered a hypothetical in which a CEO complains that he can’t do something because “I’m fighting a board who doesn’t want to do this.” That tells an intelligence asset who the obstacle is. The service then asks, “Who’s the sticking point here?” and looks for ways into that person’s email and phone.

What a rival intelligence service wants is often less technology than policy insight, including who’s pushing to change export rules and who the biggest blocker is. “Intel world tends to be like cancer,” he noted. “Once it gets into the body, it looks to spread and looks to reach out.”.

The playbook isn’t upcoming, Eftimiades added, “particularly for China.” Any executive dealing with the country “will tell you that they’ve been approached.” He stated there are also “tons of diplomat stories” of U.S. diplomats walking into a hotel room to find a woman on the bed. He said what’s newer compared with Soviet era spying is the relationships these services cultivate now often last years, not weeks.

Industry observers note that technology can augment that human intelligence, Eftimiades stated, pointing to IMSI catchers as one example. The devices mimic a cell tower so that nearby phones connect to them. A basic version can cost about $1,000 and fit in a suitcase, he said, though government-grade models cost far more, and there were a couple of cases involving Chinese espionage where these factored in last year.

It has been revealed that eftimiades says no one knows yet if the devices were used against Huang, whose phone was presumably hardened such that compromises could be detected, if not stopped altogether. But what Nvidia’s security team knew, and whether it could have acted on it, will only become clearer as the board’s independent investigation and federal inquiries proceed.

In the meantime, Eftimiades said he hopes the whole episode is “a wake-up call” for U.S. industry, which he said is mostly “clueless” about China’s tactics. “We have lost trillions [of dollars] in intellectual property,” is his guess. “Whatever we think we’re doing isn’t working.”.

Here's what actually happens if your laptop battery is completely drained

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A dead battery might do more damage than you think.
  • If your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger.
  • It has been revealed that granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A dead battery might do more damage than you think.

If your laptop has ever run out of battery unexpectedly, you know what an inconvenience it can be — especially if you're out in the world without a charger. One minute you're cranking away on some crucial spreadsheet for work, and the next, you're staring at your own face reflected in a black screen. Aside from the jump scare of the latter, there could actually be a bigger risk to letting your laptop battery completely drain.

It has been revealed that granted, there's a lot of information on the internet about the best ways to take care of your battery. Some of it hinges on the type of battery and how you use it. No matter how you cut it, though, a total drain isn't ideal, even if it won't set off a disaster if it happens from time to time. Nevertheless, here's what happens when you fully drain your laptop battery.

Industry observers note that on the whole, lithium-ion batteries, like those you'd find in a laptop, are pretty low maintenance and have several perks, such as being able to charge fairly quickly. In a perfect world, you wouldn't get all the way down to 0%. HP explains that if you want to extend your laptop battery's life as long as possible, it's best to keep the charge somewhere between 20% and 80%. Others might recommend charging to 40% to 80%. Either way, this also takes a bite out of the myth that you should drain your battery before recharging it in the name of longevity.

Repeatedly letting your battery drop to low levels can cause wear to the battery. Staying within a safe range helps keep the lithium ions in a stable state. Battery degradation could affect charging capacity. It should also be noted that some systems, like Windows, will actually shut down or hibernate before your battery hits 0%.

Sources indicate that if you find yourself flirting with that 0% a little more often than you'd like, it might be worth investigating whether there are reasons your battery is draining faster than normal. Most current laptops will last between 4 and 12 hours on a single charge, with some lasting even longer. This will vary depending on your laptop and what you're doing with it. For instance, gaming laptops won't last as long.

Otherwise, you could have apps running in the background that you don't need. Depending on the laptop you have, you might have some energy options to check out and tweak. Older software, higher temperatures or even plugged-in devices could all be contributing to your battery drain.

Recent findings suggest that in any case, it's worth keeping an eye on how much battery you have left if you're not connected to your charger. On the whole, draining your battery is mostly a self-inflicted annoyance. It's also not something you want to make a regular habit of doing, particularly if you're interested in making your battery last as long as possible.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that we’ve been reviewing a bunch of new gadgets and hardware at TechCrunch this year: dumb phones, bird feeders, health trackers, slushy machines, AI mattress pads, you name it. Sometimes we think they’re unnecessary and expensive, but other times, we try out devices that we love so much that we go out and buy them ourselves.

If these products can impress a group of (sometimes) curmudgeonly tech reporters, then they’re sure to please whoever you’re shopping for this holiday season.

Industry observers note that we’ve reviewed a lot of e-readers this year. What can we say? We’re nerds. We work for a tech website. But after trying devices from the usual suspects as well as some wildcards, we have recommendations. Evidently, 2026 was the year we fell in love with the pocket-sized e-reader.

It’s an e-reader so small that it can fit in your wallet, or even magnetize to the back of your phone. Do you dream of a world where instead of scrolling Instagram when you’re waiting in line for coffee, you actually opt to read books? There’s really something special about the X3, and it’s only $55 during Xteink’s Black Friday sale. Fair warning, it takes some fiddling with to set up, and it has no integration with Kindle, Libby, or any other apps, so only buy this for someone willing to do a bit of Reddit browsing and tinkering to get it up and running.

Sources indicate that if you aren’t planning to magnetize the XTeink to your phone, you’ve got to go with the X4 Pro. It’s slightly bigger, but it has a backlight, which makes it way more versatile. After using both the X3 and the X4 Pro, I find that the backlight really is a game changer, since I do a lot of reading in bed — plus, I like my Pop Socket wallet a bit too much to displace for the X3, and I’d rather just carry an extra credit card-sized device than risk forgetting my actual credit and ID cards, which I have grown too used to having on my phone.

Sources indicate that if I’m being honest, reading my colleague Aisha Malik’s review of the Boox Palma Pro 2 is making me want to buy one. I love using the Xteink e-readers, but they don’t connect to any outside apps. As a hardcore Libby power user (a phrase I am saying in earnest sincerity), it’s a bit frustrating that I can’t get my library books on Xteink e-readers. The same goes for apps like Kobo and Kindle, where any e-book you already own cannot be transferred out of the Amazon ecosystem unless the publisher agrees, which most do not.

If you’re looking for an e-reader with a screen that’s actually book-sized, my favorite that I’ve used is the Kobo Libra Colour, which is $259. The Amazon Paperwhite line is great, but c’mon, Amazon. Branch out!

Industry observers note that hey, we’ve all got to eat. And if you want, you can make that eating process overly techy. Why not?

In a recent development, the Ember Mug 3 is the latest iteration in Ember’s line of coffee/tea cups that actually stay warm. Our reviewer Lauren Forristal especially appreciated that you no longer need to use your phone app to change the mug’s temperature, which seems like it would be really annoying!

This mug is perfect for gifting to someone, or to put on your own wishlist — you might not want to spend $99 on a mug for yourself, but these sorts of luxury, nice-to-haves are what holidays are made for!

Ah, Ninja, the premiere firm in the business of turning every appliance into a two-in-one air fryer. I jest, but at least Ninja knows it’s onto something. Despite the high price point, Lauren says that this new product made “a pretty convincing case for ditching two appliances and making room for one.” You can’t buy more counter space (without moving), but you can buy more versatile appliances.

Sources indicate that sure, there are cheaper ice makers on the market. But Aisha clarifies that this is the ice maker for “those who crave what’s called ‘the good ice.’” If you feel so passionately about the ice in your beverages that you know what she means, then maybe this is for you.

What they really want is a Mac mini or Claude subscription, but if that’s out of budget, we have some other ideas that might impress your AI-pilled, vibe-coder loved ones….

When I asked my colleague Lucas Ropek what about his favorite product he reviewed this year, he mentioned the Codex Micro. Some hard-core coders — who the product is aimed toward — have found this thing less than pleasing, but Lucas seems to have had fun figuring out this first attempt by OpenAI at hardware.

According to recent reports, best case, it’s a productivity game-changer for your friend who has a hardworking team of AI agents within the OpenAI ecosystem. Worst case, this will be a great piece of tech history in a few years.

As people have become more conscious about how much time they spend online, new tech has emerged that, ironically, is designed to keep you away from tech. Some of these products can really make a difference in your life.

In a recent development, for about six months, I’ve consistently used the Brick to prevent me from using social media as the last thing I do before bed, or the first thing in the morning. Some people use it to help them focus during the work day, but evidently, I was not the only one who needed Brick’s help with sleep. The organization recently introduced its second device, Brick Night, which “Bricks” your phone when you are in the same room. You can customize the times that the Brick Night is active, so it’s not as though you can never, ever use social media in your room. Both Brick and Brick Night are very customizable, so you can create the perfect set-up tailored to your needs.

It’s embarrassing how whole-heartedly I recommend the Brick, which is basically just a hunk of plastic with an NFC chip in it and a companion app. But my sleep has improved significantly — I even do 8 AM Pilates now. Who am I?

In a recent development, I’ve tried out far pricier smart phone alternatives, but the Dumb Phone was both the most affordable, and the most usable for me. In the humble shell of a $20 TCL flip phone, Dumb Co loads its own software so that users can access apps like WhatsApp, Spotify, Apple Music, and Uber. You can even access iMessage through a third-party app, though Apple could probably get that shut down… no one tell Apple, please!

The Dumb Phone is particularly usable because it’s not intended to be a complete replacement for your smartphone — it’s more like a companion device that you can take out with you when you want to feel more present in the world but still may need to call an Uber home.

Wearable health trackers are pretty common nowadays, but after reviewing several different rings and wristbands, Aisha has named a winner.

There are a lot of ugly health trackers. And then there’s the Oura Ring 5, the leading smart ring maker’s first product that’s thin enough to wear without loudly broadcasting to the world that you’re monitoring your heart rate. (For what it’s worth, I tried the RingConn 3 — which is about the same size as Oura Ring 5 — but returned it, unsatisfied. Womp womp.) Aisha notes in her review that the newest Oura ring is more durable, has a better battery life, and looks more premium than its predecessors.

Sources indicate that the NYT's latest daily word game has become a social media hit. The Times credits associate puzzle editor Wyna Liu with helping to create the new word game and bringing it to the publications' Games section. Connections can be played on both web browsers and mobile devices and require players to group four words that share something in common.

Each puzzle features 16 words and each grouping of words is split into four categories. These sets could comprise of anything from book titles, software, country names, etc. Even though multiple words will seem like they fit together, there's only one correct answer.

If a player gets all four words in a set correct, those words are removed from the board. Guess wrong and it counts as a mistake—players get up to four mistakes until the game ends.

Industry observers note that players can also rearrange and shuffle the board to make spotting connections easier. Additionally, each group is color-coded with yellow being the easiest, followed by green, blue, and purple. Like Wordle, you can share the results with your friends on social media.

Starship flight 15 powers to orbit—setting up a possible catch on Saturday

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.
  • Recent findings suggest that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon.
  • The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

STARBASE, Texas—Starship lifted off right on schedule Friday from South Texas, making its 15th test flight in more than three years.

Recent findings suggest that the largely successful launch took place in the early evening; as the massive rocket rose into the atmosphere, the Sun sank toward the western horizon. Conditions were ideal for the launch, with the atmospheric winds so calm the rocket’s white plume did not dissipate for many minutes. The weather in South Texas is not always comfortable; summers are long and hot. Friday evening was perfect at Starbase.

The first stage ascended toward space flawlessly, releasing the upper stage above the Gulf of Mexico. From there, the Starship upper stage ignited its Raptor engines and powered its way into a nominal orbit. This was the second time SpaceX has flown Starship into low-Earth orbit.

When it came time for the first stage to return to the ground, it dropped like a rock. However, due to an unspecified problem, the vehicle was commanded to divert into the Gulf rather than return to the Starbase facility to be caught by the launch tower. It created a fantastically powerful explosion, even for observers more than 10 miles away.

Sources indicate that the primary aim of Friday’s launch was the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites from a narrow door at the base of the spacecraft. This occurred about 40 minutes into Starship’s flight, and all 26 satellites—which have solar panels that stretch 60 meters end to end when fully deployed—safely made it into orbit, where they will now use onboard propulsion to raise their altitude.

Industry observers note that this means that Starship is now an operational, orbital rocket. It is the largest and most powerful machine humans have ever launched into space. The challenge for the company now is to make Starship reusable and dramatically increase its flight rate.

It has been revealed that in that sense, the first part of Friday’s mission was not a success. SpaceX had hoped to return the first-stage booster, refurbish it, and fly it again. The firm has previously landed and reflown Starship boosters but has yet to do so with the latest iteration of the vehicle, version 3.

In a recent development, however, SpaceX still has a chance to make history on Saturday with the potential return of the Starship upper stage. SpaceX has never attempted to catch the vehicle’s upper stage.

Doing so will require Starship to pass a series of tests in orbit and subsequently during its return to Earth to ensure it is fully healthy. This is critical because Starship will be passing over parts of Mexico and the United States before returning to Starbase, and SpaceX does not want to endanger people on the ground. Additionally, it does not want to risk damage to its launch towers.

Industry observers note that if Starship passes these health checks, it would land at about 3:15 pm local time in Texas (21:15 UTC). If it does not, the company has earlier options to de-orbit the vehicle into an ocean.

It has been revealed that successfully returning Starship’s upper stage would be historic, as well as significant for SpaceX’s efforts to reuse the massive rocket. It would also give the organization valuable information about the vehicle’s performance during reentry.

Sources indicate that one of the biggest hurdles left in Starship’s development is the vehicle’s heat shield, which must protect the upper stage during its return through Earth’s atmosphere. More than that, SpaceX aims to make Starship rapidly reusable, and to do this, Starship’s tiles must be light and resilient.

SpaceX has been experimenting with tiles since the beginning of the Starship program, trying to find the right combination of low mass, heat resistance, and durability so the tiles require minimal refurbishment between launches. For this flight, SpaceX said it is applying learnings from the previous test flight in September, including additional retention mechanisms on tiles in areas deemed to be at the highest risk of falling off during ascent and addressing areas with a flow path for plasma to get behind the tiles.

Another problem on recent flights has been heat incursion into the small gaps between the edges of the tiles. According to SpaceX, this Starship has a large portion of the heat shield equipped with a curved tile design that has shown the ability to reduce heating in the gaps between tiles.

#56. Tech Report: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (704 w)
📖 Baca
EV & Auto ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: What causes a sudden drop in phone battery percentage?

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (704 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An aging battery or a recent software enhancement could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.
  • Recent findings suggest that few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual.
  • According to recent reports, at the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An aging battery or a recent software enhancement could be the reasons behind your phone's sudden battery drops.

Recent findings suggest that few things are more frustrating than noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster than usual. It gets to a point where it can no longer last a full day away from the charger. Under normal conditions, battery drain depends on what you're doing on your phone. Lighter uses like browsing the web and listening to music use less power, while taking lots of photos and playing games tend to drain your battery faster. But when your phone's battery suddenly drops without heavy use, something might be wrong.

According to recent reports, at the same time, that doesn't mean your phone's battery is dying. Software can also cause your battery to drain faster, like when you install an iOS or Android patch, or when an app is constantly running in the background. If you've been noticing that your phone's battery is draining faster, here's what you can try to fix it.

Sources indicate that your phone doesn't know exactly how much charge is left in the battery. In fact, it estimates that number based on the battery's voltage and current, and sometimes that estimate is far off from reality. Eventually, the software recalculates it, and that's when you see the battery percentage suddenly drop by a significant amount instead of gradually. This happens more often with batteries in poor condition. As lithium-ion batteries age chemically, they no longer retain their full charge capacity and may also fail when the phone needs a power boost to perform a demanding task, like opening the camera or using GPS. As a result, your phone may think the battery is much lower than it actually is.

It has been revealed that smartphones have mechanisms to prevent this from happening. On iPhones, Apple has implemented a system that detects when the battery fails to reduce performance in order to avoid these spikes in power consumption. Temperature also has a major impact, as most phones are rated to operate at temperatures between 0° and 35° C (32° to 95° F). Using your phone at temperatures above that range can significantly reduce battery life. When your phone gets too hot, the battery will most likely drain much faster. It's best to stop using it until it returns to a normal temperature. Don't put it in a refrigerator, though, as the introduction of cold air can create condensation within the warmer phone.

Sources indicate that also, it's perfectly normal to see your phone's battery drain a little faster for a few hours or even days after an update. Both iOS and Android run a series of optimizations to put all the files in their proper places, and this increases battery consumption. The good news is that this is temporary, and everything goes back to normal once the indexing process is complete. A buggy app or a process constantly running in the background, especially if it uses your location, will also drain your phone's battery promptly.

Start by closing apps running in the background to see if your battery usage returns to normal. It's also worth taking a look at your privacy settings and limiting access to your location to only when you have an app open. This prevents your phone from constantly triggering the GPS. That alone should have a significant impact on reducing battery consumption. Also, check your phone's battery settings to see exactly which apps are draining your battery the most — both iOS and Android provide details on this.

Pixel 6 and later models have a Battery Diagnostics tool under Settings. On a Samsung Galaxy, open Settings, then Battery and tap View Details. For iPhone owners, it's as simple as going to Settings and opening the Battery menu. These menus usually include details about your phone's battery health. Apple, for example, says that the latest iPhones are designed to retain 80 percent of their original battery capacity through up to 1,000 charge cycles. If your phone's battery health is below 80 percent, you should probably replace it with a upcoming one — which, at least, is much cheaper than buying a new phone.

Meta is entering the increasingly competitive real-time speech-to-text market with Muse Voice Transcribe, a latest audio perception model that combines streaming transcription, endpoint detection and speaker diarization for more than 20 speakers — at a public API price of just $0.18 per hour of processed audio.

Developed by Meta Superintelligence Labs, Muse is designed to process speech while it happens rather than waiting for a recording to finish. Meta’s launch post for Muse Voice Transcribe notes the model supports long audio exceeding an hour, seamless multilingual code-switching, language and keyword biasing, and diarization without a separate post-processing pipeline. The model was trained across more than 70 languages, with 25 extensively validated for the initial release.

In a recent development, the 20-plus-speaker figure is substantial, but it is not a world record. A review of current vendor documentation turns up systems with higher published ceilings. Speechmatics' real-time transcription service notes it can identify 50 speakers by default and up to 100 when the limit is increased, while Amazon Transcribe's diarization documentation specifies a maximum of 30 unique speakers, including for streaming transcription. (Speechmatics).

Muse nevertheless lands toward the high end of the market, and Meta's broader proposition is arguably more crucial than the raw maximum: high-capacity real-time diarization combined with low-latency transcription, endpointing, multilingual code-switching and aggressive API pricing in the same model.

For enterprise developers building meeting systems, call analytics, live assistants or ambient AI, that combination could matter more than who holds the speaker-count record.

According to recent reports, traditional speech recognition answers a relatively simple question: What was remarked? Diarization adds another: Who said it?

That distinction becomes critical as transcripts feed downstream AI systems. A meeting assistant can correctly transcribe every sentence and still create an unreliable corporate record if it attributes an approval, commitment or objection to the wrong participant. The same concern affects customer-service analytics, compliance workflows and AI agents operating in rooms where several people can speak.

Muse incorporates speaker attribution directly into its autoregressive multimodal architecture. Meta states audio arrives in 80-millisecond chunks, or 12.5 chunks per second, with each transformed into a soft token. At each step, the model decides whether to consume more audio or emit text. Meta calls this mechanism adaptive delay: rather than applying one latency budget to every word, Muse can wait longer when speech is ambiguous and commit earlier when it has enough context. Meta says reinforcement learning combines word-error-rate and delay rewards to train that behavior. Meta's technical explanation of Muse details the architecture. (Meta AI Research).

Speaker attribution and endpointing then become part of the same token sequence. A <|start_of_turn|> token marks a potential new speaker turn, tokens such as <|speaker_A|> identify the speaker, and separate onset and endpoint tokens identify speech boundaries. Meta claims it trains ASR, diarization and endpointing together rather than running speaker clustering as an unrelated downstream process.

Meta's Model API speech-to-text documentation also exposes diarization as a first-class operating mode alongside push-to-talk and endpointing. Speaker labels such as A and B are scoped to a session rather than verified identities, and the API provides turn-level rather than word-level timestamps.

Speaker-count comparisons require care because vendors implement diarization differently and do not all publish a maximum.

Speechmatics currently makes the strongest explicit real-time capacity claim found in this review. Its real-time STT documentation says speaker diarization is available live, while its real-time FAQ says the system supports 50 speakers by default and can be increased to 100.

AWS likewise exceeds Meta's stated figure: Amazon Transcribe can differentiate a maximum of 30 unique speakers, and AWS provides explicit instructions for speaker partitioning in a streaming transcription.

In a recent development, soniox supports diarization in both real-time and asynchronous processing, but documents a maximum of 15 speakers per session. AssemblyAI's streaming diarization system lets developers set max_speakers between one and 10. Both companies caution that live speaker attribution is more difficult because streaming systems must make decisions with less future audio context than offline models.

Recent findings suggest that xAI's current Speech-to-Text API also supports speaker diarization in streaming mode, but its documentation reviewed for this story does not publish a maximum diarized-speaker count, so a direct ceiling comparison with Muse is not possible. (X.ai Docs).

Industry observers note that that means it would be inaccurate to describe Muse's 20-plus capability as a fresh global record. The highest explicitly documented real-time number identified in this survey is Speechmatics' configurable 100-speaker ceiling.

Meta also does not demonstrate 20-plus simultaneous participants in its launch material. Its principal live demonstration uses eight speakers, while its long-form recording contains 11 labeled participants. The 20-plus number is a stated model capability rather than the participant count in the public demos.

Meta's pricing makes the competitive picture more interesting.

In a recent development, according to its Muse Voice Transcribe developer page, Muse costs $3 per 1,000 minutes, or $0.18 per hour. Streaming and non-streaming transcription cost the same, and Meta claims zero-data-retention processing is priced at parity with standard processing. Billing applies to audio actually processed and is rounded down to whole seconds.

Standardizing publicly posted rates to one hour of streaming audio gives the following rough comparison:.

Industry observers note that the comparison is necessarily imperfect. Qwen's price varies by deployment geography; its international real-time rate of $0.00009 per second works out to about $0.324 per hour. Google's Gemini figure is an estimated blended token cost rather than a flat hourly tariff. AWS prices vary by region and usage tier. ElevenLabs lists $0.39 per hour on its API pricing page but advertises $0.28 per hour or lower on annual Business looks.

It has been revealed that deepgram's pricing particularly illustrates why feature-level comparisons matter: its current Nova-3 Multilingual streaming rate is about $0.35 per hour, but speaker diarization costs another $0.002 per minute, bringing the comparable total to roughly $0.47 per hour. AssemblyAI similarly lists $0.45 per hour for Universal-3.5 Pro Realtime and another $0.12 per hour for streaming diarization.

Cartesia is harder to normalize because Ink-2 is packaged through monthly credit plans rather than a simple metered PAYG hourly rate. Its $5 Pro strategy includes roughly nine hours and 16 minutes of Ink-2 transcription, which works out to about $0.54 per transcription hour if every credit is consumed exclusively on STT. That should not be treated as equivalent to a standalone $0.54 hourly API tariff.

Sources indicate that even with those caveats, Muse's positioning is clear. It is not the absolute cheapest streaming transcription service — Soniox presently publishes a lower equivalent rate — but $0.18 per hour with diarization included puts Meta toward the low end of the market, especially against providers that charge separately for speaker attribution.

At 1,000 hours of processed audio, Meta's public rate implies roughly $180 in transcription charges.

Price matters less if it comes with a large accuracy penalty. Meta's benchmark material argues the opposite.

On the Artificial Analysis AA-WER Streaming Index supplied with the launch, Muse records a 3.1% final-transcription word error rate, ahead of Cartesia Ink-2 at 3.4%, ElevenLabs Scribe v2 Realtime at 3.6%, Qwen3 ASR Flash Realtime at 3.7%, GPT Live Transcribe and Grok Speech to Text Streaming at 3.9%, and Gemini 3.5 Transcribe Live and AssemblyAI U3.5 Realtime Pro at 4.0%.

Meta points out that Muse took the number one spot on third-party independent AI benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis' streaming speech-to-text evaluation as of September 1. Meta published the following benchmark charts in its launch post.

In a recent development, its diarization result may be even more relevant to the product's positioning. Meta reports an average 17.5% diarization error rate across AMI-IHM, AMI-SDM and VoxConverse, lower than the competing systems shown in its chart.

Speaker capacity and diarization error rate should not be conflated. A platform capable of representing 100 people is not automatically better at correctly attributing speech than one supporting 20, and Meta's benchmark does not test every competitor operating at its advertised maximum speaker count.

It has been revealed that there are deployment tradeoffs as well. Meta's API at the moment provides turn-level but not word-level timestamps, and it does not expose word-level confidence scores, sound-event detection or emotion detection. The documentation also specifies eight concurrent streams per tenant by default and real-time sessions of up to 60 minutes before an application must reconnect.

Still, Muse's launch creates an unusually sharp price-performance proposition. Its 20-plus-speaker diarization does not establish a world record, but the record may be the less important metric. For enterprise developers, the larger question is whether a service can preserve speaker attribution, accurate text and usable turn boundaries while a complicated real-world conversation is still unfolding.

At $0.18 per hour, with 20-plus-speaker diarization inside the same real-time model that currently leads Meta's supplied streaming accuracy benchmarks, Muse Voice Transcribe gives enterprise teams a serious latest option for meeting intelligence, live transcription and voice-agent infrastructure — while putting additional pressure on competitors to compete on speaker-aware accuracy and total operating cost, not merely raw speech recognition.

#54. This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (940 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

This AI Tamagotchi Turns Everyday Objects Into Needy Virtual Pets

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected.
  • That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects.
  • In a recent development, you might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

You forgot to water the plant. Instead of seeing yellowing leaves, you see a cute plant-shaped pet on a tiny screen, looking sad and dejected. Maybe that'll give you the push you needed to grab the watering can. As you pour water into the soil, the plant pet on the screen gets excited and happy.

That's the idea behind OATs, or Object Agent Twins—micro-agent AI avatars on tiny E Ink displays designed to pair with everyday household objects. The tech was created by Daehwa Kim, a fifth-year PhD student in Carnegie Mellon's Future Interfaces Group. Kim presented the project at the ACM Symposium on User Interface Software and Technology in Detroit in early November, a forum where academics and industry experts explore human-computer interfaces, and she earned two Honorable Mention awards.

In a recent development, you might remember Tamagotchi, the popular egg-shaped toys from the ’90s that housed digital pets requiring real-time care and attention. Kim’s goal was to bring a similar experience to physical objects in our lives. “We bring this joy of caring from virtual to physical objects,” she tells WIRED. While folks have encouraged Kim to sell OAT kits online, she hasn't decided whether to pursue it as a business opportunity.

Kim notes everyone spends all day staring at mobile devices, and AI agents—even if they're designed to handle tasks on your behalf—still demand attention from your smartphone screen. OATs were a way to bring those interactions out into the real world.

Giving AI a physical body isn't fresh, as companies rush to create “the next smartphone,” whether that's failed attempts like the Humane Ai Pin, OpenAI's upcoming hardware created in collaboration with famed ex-Apple designer Jony Ive, or Meta's Muse Charm. The pocket-sized gadget houses Meta's popular Muse AI agent and is expected to launch in December. Increasingly, though, companies have leaned on “cuteness” in their strategy for widespread adoption.

OATs have an E Ink display connected to internal and external sensors that can track things like moisture, temperature, humidity, light, occupancy, and motion. (The hardware is relatively cheap, around $20 for the main module.) The sprites are created with Google Gemini's Nano Banana image-generation service, creating a suite of emotions for various states based on the sensor data. You can set all of this up through a web portal, where you can name your OAT and choose which sensors to use for the object you're attaching it to.

The web app will generate “Positive” and “Negative” behaviors based on your object's name and description. So if the OAT is attached to a plant, positive triggers could be “consistent air temperature readings” and “low humidity levels” if the plant of choice prefers dry environments. However, you can customize these behaviors to suit your specific plant type.

Recent findings suggest that it can be used for very simple things. Want to use your skateboard more often? Attach the OAT to your board, and if it hasn't detected motion for a few days, the avatar will look sad and lonely. You don't want that, do you? As Kim notes, “These kinds of inanimate objects can be more expressive.” When you hop on the board, the OAT avatar will be happy, with fun faces.

The catch is that the system's battery life is really short, showing why this is more of a proof of concept than anything else. OATs last around three to four days, but paired with the sound-level sensor, they'll only last a day. It has a USB-C port for charging the lithium-ion polymer battery.

Recent findings suggest that kim notes she distributed OATs to many people and found that they used them in three different ways. One is, “Am I being used?” Like when you attach an OAT to a coffee machine and have the avatar get excited when the machine starts grinding beans. The second is for warning people near an object. For example, 3D printers release toxic fumes during use, and attaching an OAT to one can warn people that the device is operational. And the third is to track their own behaviors. Someone attached an OAT to a dumbbell to track how often they lifted weights, encouraging themselves to exercise regularly so they wouldn't disappoint the AI pet.

The demo at the symposium was popular, and Kim turned it into a competition to see who could come up with the most interesting ideas about what objects to pair with the OATs. Kim's website features a gallery with sprites people made, from an animated conference badge to a panda avatar for an Owala water bottle.

But the demo also ignited a huge discussion about anthropomorphizing artificial intelligence, and whether it’s proper to give these sprites humanlike traits and emotions to make people feel connected with them.

According to recent reports, it's already a topic in play within the AI industry. Companies often refer to their chatbot behaviors in human terms, like when they “hallucinate.” Anthropic announced a “dreaming” feature this summer where its AI agent cleaned up its local memory as a background process. These anthropomorphized terms can distort moral judgments about AI and cause people to overly trust the tools.

Kim says that's why OATs have very limited interactions, restricted to expressive emotions and the E Ink display.

“Anthropomorphism can be very useful in certain ways, like helping people to change their behaviors,” Kim says. “People name their car, and they name their bike. I rarely see people who name their iPhone. I feel like in the future of computing we will have more of a relationship with AI, but we should definitely be careful not to abuse this.".

There are a ton of great 3-in-1 chargers, with latest ones flooding the market daily, but very few combine this level of portability with all the features we discussed.

Sources indicate that so if you are shopping for a portable 3-in-1 travel charger for yourself or as a gift, I would highly recommend giving this one a shot. It’s well-built, charges your substantial three Apple products, and looks fantastic.
