📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I am traveling through Portugal now that Web Summit has wrapped up, so please enjoy this shortened edition.

Web Summit leaned heavily into Chinese founders and companies this year. The opening remarks from Web Summit co-founder Paddy Cosgrave drove the point home when he stated the superstars of the future are coming from China, not California. He also gave a strong endorsement of China and open source technology when he noted that Chinese companies are building more of our shared future than anyone else.

These remarks carried a different kind of weight just a few days later as the news spread throughout the conference that Nvidia founder and CEO Jensen Huang had resigned from his leadership post after admitting to an affair with an alleged spy.

The former CEO, after all, has been one of the strongest proponents for open source in the United States. And anyone who has followed the emergence of autonomous vehicle tech knows how central Nvidia is to that ecosystem.

Nvidia is a major supplier of AI computing technology to the industry — although the degree of reliance varies. Some companies are using Nvidia’s automotive processors to run automated driving software, while others are using Nvidia GPUs to train autonomous driving models. And then there are the full-stack partnerships, which includes Mercedes-Benz, Zoox, and Wayve.

I spoke to Leo Wang, the CFO of Chinese autonomous vehicle manufacturer Pony.ai, this week. I asked him about the challenges China’s self-driving industry faces and what he thinks will happen if the fallout from Huang’s resignation results in even stricter export controls on Nvidia chips shipped to China.

Recent findings suggest that demand is already far greater than supply, Wang said, noting that it’s one of the pain points Pony.ai struggles with. The company’s strategy is twofold. Engineers are directed to be as efficient as possible when deploying its training models. That might mean using midtier compute resources instead of high-end ones, he said.

Pony.ai is also turning more to domestically produced chips to help close the gap.

Industry observers note that “If you look at the whole ecosystem, especially in recent years, definitely domestic chips in China also get lots of attention and development,” he said, noting that these chips provide another option for AI training. “I think that gives us some flexibility.”.

When asked what he thinks will happen if export restrictions on Nvidia chips tighten, Wang mentioned Chinese companies have already been preparing.

It has been revealed that “If you look at the whole situation, this has been developing for already a couple of years,” he stated. “Everyone, I would say, is also practicing kind of like a Plan B for a few years, so at least if you think about that, I would say there are alternatives. Although cost-effectiveness-wise, probably it’s not the best choice yet. But still, it’s an alternative way that already exists and which is more mature than a few years ago.”.

It has been revealed that may Mobility looks to use the Volkswagen all-electric ID. Buzz for its global ride-hailing platform. The company mentioned it is targeting the deployment of more than 10,000 autonomous vehicles through 2031. This does not mean that VW’s MOIA group is ditching Mobileye, I have been told. Instead, VW told me, the company is offering an automated driving-ready base vehicle to other companies that develop their own self-driving systems. (This was just presented last month during Nvidia GTC in Berlin.).

Newmo, a Japanese robotaxi startup, raised a ¥20.8 billion (roughly $135 million) round led by KDDI.

ParkBee, a Dutch parking technology firm, acquired Mobian’s city and parking operations.

Port, an urban logistics organization, raised €14.5 million in a round led by the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD) and Balnord.

Sources indicate that lucid reported Q3 revenue of $350 million, below Wall Street expectations, and it is still losing money. Although its Q3 net loss did narrow to $830.9 million. Notably, the EV maker increased its delayed draw term loan from its largest shareholder, Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, to $1.75 billion.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration is investigating a Waymo software recall from a year ago that was issued after numerous reports that its robotaxis were illegally passing school buses. The agency mentioned that a majority of these reported incidents occurred after the company deployed a software revision intended to fix the problem. Sources familiar with Waymo tell me that there have not been school bus-related incidents since March. I have not been able to independently verify that with the Austin Independent School District.

The Tesla Cybertruck will live on through next summer, but production will ultimately end, according to Elon Musk, who defended the polarizing steel-clad truck.

Tesla is expanding its robotaxi service to San Antonio, Texas, as it seeks to compete with Waymo and position itself as more than just an automaker.

Uber is launching a new service that lets customers reserve and pay for parking in major U.S. cities, about nine months after the ride-hailing tech giant acquired parking app SpotHero. Meanwhile, the company is notifying thousands of drivers that their personal and driver’s license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company’s tech providers.

Smart home tech often relies solely on cloud connections and pricey AI subscriptions, but UGREEN is delivering a local-first solution in its latest HomeAgent collection, delivering cameras, speakers, and more that bring the bulk of the functionality and processing directly to your home.

According to recent reports, the UGREEN AIoT – AI of Things – ecosystem is built around pairing hardware to a central hub that acts as your home’s brain. The HomeAgent HA100 and Pro are that “brain,” pairing to smart home gear such as lights, speakers, and cameras to not only store recordings, but process the data locally.

At the core of the experience is UGREEN’s Uliya AI assistant, which you can talk to directly through HomeAgent HA100 or through a connected Smart Speaker for Uliya. The assistant can handle simple tasks like controlling lights or playing music, of course, but can do a lot more with video recordings. You can ask questions such as “is there a package outside” or “where is my dog” and Uliya will be able to parse through camera recordings to find the answer rather than forcing you to have to scroll through timelines.

That’s all powered by the HomeAgent HA100. It can also acts as network storage for photos, household files, and more, all of which can be used as context for the local AI system – and there’s no monthly fee to store or access it.

According to recent reports, UGREEN’s hardware lineup around the HomeAgent centerpieces includes cameras such as the SynCare cameras. These deliver the local recording capabilities that are so central to the system. SynCare OD800 Pro is a triple-lens outdoor camera with solar power and a built-in battery, while the OD600 Pro delivers the same powerful camera setup with power-over-ethernet. These have an 8MP primary camera and dual 5MP cameras with pan-tilt-zoom capabilities. They can zoom in up to 9x, feature motion tracking and a built-in spotlight, as well as color night vision and IP66 dust/water protection.

Meanwhile, the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro is a pan-tilt-zoom camera meant to be used inside to capture events in an entire room. It features 4K imaging, 360-degree pan and 160-degree vertical tilt while supporting up to 8x digital zoom, motion tracking, and even baby-cry detection. It also has a physical shutter for your privacy.

There are also two smart frames, the UGREEN Gallery E-Paper Smart Frame mounts on the wall to display photos and artwork, while the UGREEN Gallery LCD Smart Frame can sit on a table or hang on the wall, showing photos and videos, while also integrating with the rest of your smart home’s functions.

UGREEN has its own smart speaker for the system, and you can also integrate select Matter hardware as well, including smart lighting, robot vacuums and other smart home devices.

The UGREEN HomeAgent ecosystem will start at $799 for a limited time when its Kickstarter campaign launches on April 13, 2027, with upgraded packages that drastically increase AI processing power, storage, and the types of devices you can connect to the system.

Industry observers note that you can reserve your UGREEN HomeAgent today to lock in early bird pricing. Reservations are open from September 4, 2026, through April 12, 2027, and deposits can be canceled for a refund any time before the campaign ends. Shipping will begin in late June 2027, with different phases for different products.

#49. 10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1858 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

10 things your iPhone's Notes app can do other than taking notes

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1858 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.
  • Industry observers note that for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live.
  • It has been revealed that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple Notes has a lot of tricks you might not have properly explored.

Industry observers note that for most people, the Notes app is where grocery lists, stray thoughts and various codes go to live. If you've only used it for basic text, you've probably missed how Apple has added new features to the mix that can solve complex equations, draw graphs, transcribe audio and turn your doodles into images. iOS 27 brought even more, including smarter Siri integration and divider lines, so the app is more capable than ever.

It has been revealed that A few of the features below rely on Apple Intelligence, requiring newer hardware to work as intended. On the iPhone, that means the iPhone 15 Pro, iPhone 15 Pro Max and any iPhone 16 model or later. Those features are flagged along the way, along with anything that requires a specific version of iOS.

The Notes app has a calculator hiding inside it, with the math happening while you're typing. Since iOS 18, when you type an equation and add an equals sign, Math Notes fills in the answer on the spot. It also works with variables, so if you write "dinner = $42" and change that value later, every result that uses it updates automatically. That makes it a surprisingly easy way to split the bill or plan a monthly budget.

Math Notes can do more than give you simple answers. After you type an equation that starts with "y =", tap the equals sign and choose Insert Graph to plot what you've typed right inside the note. If you change the variable, the graph changes automatically to match. It's a neat tool for students to check their homework without a dedicated graphing app.

Recent findings suggest that if you don't have a physical scanner at home, there's no need to download a dedicated scanner app to replace it. Tapping the attachment button in any note reveals the Scan Documents option, where Notes will capture a page automatically, including cropping and straightening it for you. The scanner also offers a flash option and image filters if needed.

In Auto mode, you don't even need to tap on the shutter button; the system captures the document once it detects the page's edges and you're holding your iPhone steady. You can scan multiple pages into a single document, which is useful for contracts, lease agreements or anything else that runs longer than a page.

In a recent development, if the document needs a signature, open the scan, tap Markup, then go to Add > Signature. Use a saved signature or draw a upcoming one with your finger, then resize it and drag it into place. It's an easy way to sign and send a form without taking a printout of the pages. Scans are saved to the note as PDFs, which you can annotate.

In a recent development, notes can double as a recorder: choose Record Audio in any note to record and transcribe everything your phone hears. The transcript is searchable, so you can jump into the relevant part of a long lecture instead of scrubbing through the entire session. On iPhone models with Apple Intelligence, Notes can summarize entire recorded lectures or meetings. Phone calls you record also land in Notes inside the Call Recordings folder with a transcript.

In a recent development, the iPhone already has a dedicated recording app in Voice Memos, so it's worth knowing when to use which. Notes is the better pick when the recording is part of something bigger. For a class or a meeting, for example, you can type your own notes, add photos of the whiteboard and keep the recording all in the same note. Everything stays together, so you won't have to switch between multiple apps when you're going through your notes at home. Meanwhile, Voice Memos makes more sense when the audio itself matters most, like an interview you blueprint to edit or share.

According to recent reports, if you need some help when drawing, sketch something rough with the Markup tools, then pick Image Wand from the same tool palette and circle your sketch. Add a few words describing the image you want, and Apple Intelligence will turn your doodle into a polished image.

In a recent development, you also have the option to circle an empty spot in the note and create a latest image based on the text around it. Afterward, fine-tune the image by adding or removing descriptive words. If your note is a packing list for a beach trip, for instance, it will generate a matching seaside illustration to sit at the top.

In iOS 27, Image Playground, which powers this feature in the Notes app, got a newly introduced model that can make photorealistic images, not just stylized ones. Since iOS 27.2, most images you generate or edit carry a SynthID watermark, which the SynthID detection website uses to know something was made by AI.

In a recent development, your notes don't have to be only for you; it's possible to share a specific note or an entire folder with your family, friends and coworkers, then everyone can make changes in real time. This is ideal for a household grocery list or a group blueprint for a trip. The person who creates the shared note remains in control of who can do what.

Just tap the Share button in the note you want to add people to, then choose whether each person can make changes or only view it. Type @ followed by someone's name and they'll get a notification pointing them to the note. If several people are editing the same note, the activity view and highlights show who changed what and when. And in iOS 27, the Shared folder now sits at the top of the folders list with a newly introduced icon, so multi-person notes are easier to spot.

Sources indicate that the Notes app can help with the actual writing you do. Select some text, tap the Apple Intelligence button in the toolbar and pick an option from the Writing Tools menu. This can proofread your text for spelling and grammar mistakes and rewrite it in a friendlier, more professional or more concise tone.

The suite is also useful for reshaping messy notes. It's able to create a summary of a long note or pull out its key points, which is handy after a meeting or before an exam. It will also turn a block of text into a bulleted list or even convert it into a table. If you've jotted down a few phone looks with their prices and data limits, for example, the Table option can organize them into neat rows and columns so they're easier to compare.

Writing Tools isn't limited to just the Notes app; it works almost anywhere you can type on the iPhone, including third-party apps. In iOS 27, Apple Intelligence also suggests ways to improve your writing.

Industry observers note that long notes quickly become messy and hard to organize, but Notes has a few tools to keep them neat. With iOS 18 and newer, you have the option to collapse any heading to minimize sections you're not working on. This means the final version is a bit cleaner to view, while it's also easier to manage everything while writing.

Recent findings suggest that if that's not enough, you can also highlight text in different colors, curating them by sections, information or any other preference. To do so, select the text, tap the Aa format button and pick a color. Notes offers five color options to choose from: pink, purple, orange, mint and blue. iOS 27 also added divider lines, which gives another option to tidy up a mess. Place your cursor where you want a break, open the edit menu and choose Insert Divider Line. If someone views the note on iOS 26 or prior, the divider lines show up as three hyphens(—), so nothing breaks.

iOS 27 also added section links to the mix, letting you link to a specific section of a note where tapping the link jumps straight there. That's particularly useful for a table of contents in a long note. Pasting Markdown now converts it to formatted text automatically, and a new Copy as Markdown option easily brings notes to other apps with the formatting intact.

Sources indicate that iOS 26 added a reed pen to the Markup tools, which is designed for a traditional calligraphy experience. Like the actual writing instrument, your strokes get thicker or thinner depending on the direction you draw in. It's a unique way to write, especially for special occasions like birthdays and invitations. You'll find the reed pen in the list of Markup tools; tapping it again after selecting it is how you pick a preset.

It has been revealed that there are five angle presets to choose from, with the one you pick deciding which stroke direction gives the thickest line. The angle is fixed no matter how you hold your finger, so your strokes stay consistent. Apart from the Notes app, the reed pen also works in Freeform, Journal and Preview — basically anywhere the Markup tools are available.

Recent findings suggest that the search bar in the Notes app is smarter than it looks and than how most people casually use it. Beyond your own typed notes, it can search handwriting, objects in images and text in scanned documents. Tap the search button, then type a word from a page or a photo. If you scanned a receipt months ago, searching for the store's name should bring it up. It's an easy way to find snippets from longer notes, especially when you're transcribing lectures or meetings.

According to recent reports, this turns your Notes library into a practical place to store paperwork you might need in the future. Consider storing information like warranty cards, appliance manuals, prescriptions and receipts all in Notes, then you can find them by searching for a word on the page instead of scrolling through dozens of scans and navigating file names.

Industry observers note that siri and Notes finally work together properly in iOS 27. Siri can create notes with generated content, like information it pulled from the web, instead of only typing what you say. Ask it to put together a packing list for a trip and save it to a new note, and it will comply. This really comes in handy for smaller notes or basic reminders, as well as capturing ideas on the spot when you can't stop to type.

It can also add to an existing note or clean up a list before saving it. If you've got a messy, unformatted list, ask Siri to tidy it up and add it to the right note. Of course, the full power of this requires Siri AI, which introduced in English first. iOS 27.2 added French, Japanese, Korean, Portuguese and Spanish. Older iPhone models can also create notes with Siri, but without the AI-generated content, which slightly limits the feature. But the basics are still there to jot down ideas.

For instance, it outperformed many large frontier models on the DeepSWE coding benchmark, at far lower cost. Meanwhile, Flash Cyber is the company’s “most capable” cybersecurity model, Pichai said; it also matches frontier-level performance when it comes to discovering vulnerabilities and patching them at scale. The model achieved 86.2% on the CyberGym cybersecurity benchmark and 47.2% on CWE-Bench, which evaluates AI patching abilities. In an internal Google benchmark, the model achieved a more than 70% success rate discovering vulnerabilities across 20 programming languages, Pichai said. 3.8 is Google’s third Flash release in six weeks and comes quickly on the heels of version 3.7. 3.8 working "harder" with "greater diligence"3.8 Flash is available now in Gemini Enterprise; devs can try it out in the Gemini API via Google AI Studio, Google Antigravity, Android Studio, or generate UIs in Stitch. It is priced at $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens — the same introductory pricing as Gemini 3.7 Flash — and people can customize and adjust model effort levels based on their needs around quality, cost, and latency. For instance, when compute efficiency is a priority, they can adjust to lower token overhead, or simply continue working with 3.7 Flash, which is “fully supported for efficiency-first workloads,” Google senior product director Tulsee Doshi and Gemini security lead Raluca Ada Popa wrote in a blog post. “3.8 Flash works harder,” exhibiting “greater diligence” with complex tasks like executing extra reasoning steps, although at times it may use more tokens to maximize performance, Doshi and Popa note. The model has a 1M-token input window and a 64K-token output limit, and can ingest text as well as images, audio, video, and PDF files. 3.8 Flash was evaluated across numerous benchmarks testing coding, multimodal capabilities, computer use, long-context and knowledge work, and scientific reasoning. Google indicates it also does well in specialized knowledge domains requiring more in-depth analysis and reporting. For instance, the model outperformed its predecessor and other frontier models on benchmarks like Vals Finance Agent V2 for finance, and Harvey's Legal Agent Benchmark for law; it also scored 54.9% on Humanity’s Last Exam (HLE)-Verified, reflecting its ability to take on multi-step reasoning tasks across subjects like math, science, and humanities. In one example shared by Google, Gemini 3.8 Flash built a game with a simple prompt using looping techniques in Google’s Antigravity platform. The game uses puzzles, storytelling that changes based on the environment, and images and textures from Nano Banana to create a 3D experience (in this case a wizard navigating a castle). In other instances, the model created a fully-functional DOS version of Google Maps featuring interactive locations, directions, and street views; a 3D visualizer that automatically decomposed devices into layers for inspection with a slider capability; and a topographic map of famous geographical sites based on real datasets from the U.S. Geological Survey, complete with real-time cross-sections, 2D projections, and scientific explanations. According to Arena.ai, 3.8 Flash landed at No. 14 in Agent Arena, ranking above DeepSeek-V4-Pro, and showed a significant jump over Gemini 3.7 Flash (which sits all the way down at No. 32). It debuted at No. 7 in Text Arena, ahead of Claude Opus 5 and Gemini 3.7 Flash. It improved over 3.7 Flash in several areas: multi-turn requests, writing, literature, and language, longer queries, hard prompts, coding, instruction following, software and IT services, and business, management and financial ops. Organizations can apply for access. Google says the model version has undergone “rigorous training” in the cybersecurity domain and represents a “significant leap in prompt injection robustness.” It is particularly adept at autonomous vulnerability discovery — at least, based on internal Gemini benchmarks — and automated patching. It is also very good at coding, Popa said in a video. The goal was to equip defenders with expert-level capabilities to give them a leg up over threat actors (whether malicious, fellow AI agents, or human hackers). “We have invested in vulnerability fixing from the start, and prioritized it over offensive capabilities like exploitation,” Doshi and Popa explain. The model ships a more permissive set of mitigations for cybersecurity safeguards — which is why, for now, it is only being shared with limited partners — and safeguards against misuse in cyber offense and areas like chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN).Google is already using 3.8 Flash Cyber to secure its own code; it produced 2.6 times more correct patches in Chrome vulnerabilities versus much larger commercial models. Wiz — which Google acquired earlier this year at a historic $32 billion — reported that 3.8 Flash Cyber had 7.5% to 9.7% higher recall of real-world vulnerabilities on an internal penetration testing benchmark at 2.3 to 5.2 times lower cost than leading frontier models. Similarly, Google’s Cloud Vulnerability Research found a critical foundational vulnerability in less than 2 hours with 3.8 Flash Cyber. Typically, that research and discovery would take months, Google claims. AI agents are “incredibly skilled” at finding and exploiting vulnerabilities, Popa said. Scanning large codebases with significant AI models is expensive, and defenders are overwhelmed. “In cybersecurity, attackers need only find one significant flaw over millions of lines of code. Defenders have to remove every one of those flaws to be able to defend against attackers.” Doug Turner, engineering director for Chrome, described a “vulnerability apocalypse” in recent months due to generative AI. “Simply overnight, we saw a hockey stick increase in the number of software vulnerabilities reported through our vulnerability research program,” he said in a video. One interesting vulnerability 3.8 Flash Cyber discovered had been in Chromium and Chrome for 13 years, he explained. It was a “very subtle bug” that dozens, if not hundreds, of engineers looked at but never flagged. “Gemini 3.8 Flash Cyber is going to allow us to create better suggested fixes so that developers’ lives can get a lot easier.”.

Following revelations about Jensen Huang’s relationship with a suspected Chinese spy Congress wants to crack down.

Unsurprisingly, following the scandal involving now-former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy, Congress is looking to further restrict exports of AI chips. Both Democrats and Republicans have voiced support for various measures and bills that would tighten rules and have demanded that Huang and other Nvidia leaders testify before Congress.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer has already mentioned that Huang and the Trump administration need to answer to Congress. Senate Banking Committee Chairman Tim Scott has also sent letters to both Huang and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick calling on them to publicly testify to the committee.

Bills such as the Remote Access Security Act, first introduced in the House in April 2025 but stalled in the Senate, are receiving renewed interest. While that specific bill might not become law, House Speaker Mike Johnson has said there is “growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China,” according to Reuters. Johnson has also said that he personally supports efforts to restrict China’s access to powerful AI chips from companies like Nvidia.

  • The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Megaspeed told CNBC Sunday that Alice Huang left the company in August 2025 and said it has launched an internal probe into media reports concerning its business and supply chain.

The Singapore-based cloud computing company has faced heightened scrutiny since former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said he had been unfaithful to his wife following reports linking him to former Megaspeed executive Alice Huang.

In a recent development, U.S. intelligence officials believe Alice Huang is a Chinese intelligence asset, according to The New York Times.

Recent findings suggest that jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia on Nov. 12 amid fallout from reports about his extramarital relationships, one of which was reportedly a direct report.

"Ms. Alice Huang officially left Megaspeed effective August 30, 2025 and currently has no role with the Manufacturer," Megaspeed said in an emailed statement shared with CNBC. "Megaspeed does not comment on Ms. Huang's personal and private matters," it added.

Megaspeed describes itself as a "core business partner" of Nvidia's computing power cloud business in the region, allowing customers to rent computing power from Nvidia GPUs, or graphics processing units — specialized chips designed to do many calculations at the same time.

The tech giant, which has offices in Singapore and Indonesia, has previously faced media and government scrutiny over whether chips supplied through its business were redirected to customers in China.

Megaspeed said Sunday that media reports about its business, supply chain and global operations are not supported by verifiable evidence and it has retained external legal counsel to conduct a "thorough internal investigation.".

"Megaspeed designs and maintains its global operational and supply-chain control frameworks to comply with all applicable laws and regulatory regimes, including United States export control requirements and local jurisdiction rules in every market where we operate," it said.

The firm added that it will review the reporting and communicate further with stakeholders as appropriate.

— CNBC's Anniek Bao and Jenni Reid helped contribute to this report.

#45. Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business

Winemakers are learning that conservation can be good for business

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that more than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes.
  • In a recent development, temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades.
  • As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that more than 500 vineyards are scattered across the slopes and valleys of South Africa’s Western Cape, one of the world’s most biologically diverse landscapes. The region produces about 90 percent of South Africa’s wine, but winemakers there are increasingly struggling with drought, excessive heat and erratic rainfall.

In a recent development, temperatures in the region have risen 1.5 to 2 times faster than the global average over the past five decades. And extreme storms have become more intense as climate variability increases. The late 2010s brought a significant challenge for winemakers, as three years of severe drought placed vineyards under intense stress and reduced grape production.

As climate variability places increasing pressure on grape production, many wine producers are building on sustainability measures that have long been part of vineyard management.

We are a team of geographers and sustainability scientists who study environmental change, environmental health, conservation, agriculture and land management. Our team wanted to better understand how farmers in South Africa’s wine-producing regions are responding as a range of environmental and economic pressures rise. We talked with growers, conservation practitioners and wine industry experts in the Western Cape and analyzed how 107 vineyards, about 20% of the total, were using sustainable land stewardship practices to adapt.

In many agricultural landscapes, production and conservation goals are frequently viewed as competing priorities. But our research found that many vineyard operators in the Western Cape see long-term stewardship and conservation of soil and wildlife habitat as essential strategies for business success.

Sources indicate that the Western Cape is home to the Cape Floral Region, a global biodiversity hot spot. It includes fynbos, a unique biome containing thousands of endemic plant species, including types of proteas, ericas and restios that are found nowhere else on Earth.

Sustainability certification and conservation programs, such as World Wildlife Fund Conservation Champions, have helped encourage vineyards to protect biodiversity in the region. Many growers use these sustainability certifications to increase their wine’s marketability. But we found they have also embraced conservation for how it can benefit their vineyards. Rather than viewing conservation as land taken out of production, many stated they see it supporting the ecological processes essential to their business.

Industry observers note that the majority of South Africa’s vineyards today participate in the Integrated Production of Wine certification system, created by the South African wine industry and researchers in 1998 to reduce environmental harm. The system sets standards governing pesticide use, water management, wastewater treatment and environmental stewardship. It also uses independent auditing of participating farms and wineries to ensure those claiming certification meet the standards.

Industry observers note that to manage the water supplies their vineyards depend on, growers described restoring native vegetation, including the removal of alien species, along waterways and reducing erosion to protect wetlands and rivers. Research shows that healthy natural systems can improve water retention in the soil and contribute to the overall resilience of the landscape in the face of more extreme climate conditions.

To boost their soil’s health, some growers are planting cover crops, such as legumes, cereals like oats and rye, and brassicas such as radish and mustard, between vine rows. Growers broadly described using cover crops, compost, mulching and other practices to improve soil structure and increase organic matter in the soil. Cover crops require maintenance and can provide habitat for pests, but research demonstrates that the right cover crops, when well maintained, can benefit vineyards by reducing erosion and increasing water retention and nutrients in the soil.

Several producers also described efforts to reduce their reliance on chemical pesticides, which is beneficial not only for the environment but also their businesses as chemical costs continue to rise. We heard about vineyards that monitor pest populations closely and respond in targeted ways rather than using pesticides broadly.

In a recent development, some growers encourage beneficial insects and manage habitats that support natural pest control. The creation of habitats for natural pest predators can reduce the overall disease risk too. While chemical treatments remain part of many vineyard operations, growers reported increasing interest in other approaches that prevent disease and pest outbreaks, such as pruning, to reduce their total chemical use.

Sustainable practices like these are well established in South Africa’s wine industry, but our interviews suggest their use has been expanding in recent years. Rather than focusing solely on treating problems after they arise, these approaches emphasize prevention, monitoring and ecological balance.

The stewardship practices we observed in South Africa are investments in long-term business resilience for many growers.

It has been revealed that many of the wine producers we interviewed described facing rising costs and market uncertainty. Exports, labor and chemicals are all expensive. They emphasized that maintaining healthy soils, conserving water and reducing vulnerability to drought and disease are essential to keeping their vineyards productive.

Industry observers note that as concerns about drought, climate pressures and profitability rise, the area in vineyard production in South Africa has also decreased. Several growers described diversifying their business models and even switching crops to make their businesses more resilient to hotter, drier conditions.

Industry observers note that farmers around the world are confronting the realities of a changing climate. Our research indicates that effective solutions can come from recognizing the interconnectedness of nature and production.

The experience of South Africa’s winegrowers shows that farms can be managed more sustainably when they’re seen as part of larger ecological systems.

Students Zoe Van der Walt, Jack Spining and Dryver Finch contributed to this article.

Sources indicate that hannah V. Herrero is Associate Professor of Geography & Sustainability and Director of Sustainability at University of Tennessee; Erin L. Bunting is Assistant Professor of Geography at Michigan State University; Jane Southworth is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; Jason K. Blackburn is Professor of Geography at University of Florida; and Stephanie Insalaco-Wyner is Assistant Professor of Geographic Information Sciences at Southwestern University.

If you like playing daily word games like Wordle, then Hurdle is a great game to add to your routine.

Recent findings suggest that there are five rounds to the game. The first round sees you trying to guess the word, with correct, misplaced, and incorrect letters shown in each guess. If you guess the correct answer, it'll take you to the next hurdle, providing the answer to the last hurdle as your first guess. This can give you several clues or none, depending on the words. For the final hurdle, every correct answer from previous hurdles is shown, with correct and misplaced letters clearly shown.

An notable note is that the number of times a letter is highlighted from previous guesses does necessarily indicate the number of times that letter appears in the final hurdle.

If you find yourself stuck at any step of today's Hurdle, don't worry! We have you covered.

Flaming Hydra’s newly introduced Kickstarter campaign rethinks e-book ownership and digital lending

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Here’s a massive promise: A upcoming Kickstarter campaign aims to usher in the “return of the human internet.”.

Industry observers note that that’s the tagline of a crowdfunding campaign for The Phoenix Project, an initiative from the online culture and commentary magazine Flaming Hydra. If you back The Phoenix Project, you’re supporting three things — a one-off print magazine designed to celebrate “the values and fun of the early internet,” a new e-book service for libraries, and a newsletter subscription/archiving program that’s also designed for libraries.

To Flaming Hydra’s lead editor Maria Bustillos, these disparate projects are “basically all one thing,” tied together by the goal of “protecting freedom of information” and fulfilling the “promise of the early internet, where you’re making information available to as many people as possible, while still protecting the right of artists and authors to make a living.”.

It has been revealed that bustillos told me that these concerns have been highlighted on Flaming Hydra itself, for example when Tal Levin wrote about finding countless AI-generated clones of his book on Amazon. By “creating an ecosystem that is based in people working together, who are offering their stuff in a context that is controlled and doesn’t allow” others to create and sell AI-generated clones, Bustillos remarked Flaming Hydra is “part of the human project.”.

In a recent development, “AI is not this unstoppable force,” she added. “If people just set up publishing pipelines and networks and organizations that are dedicated to the human internet, people who want to read stuff can go to them, and it’s actually completely isolated from mechanistic interference.”.

The Phoenix Project fits into this vision by making the work of human writers more accessible to libraries.

Recent findings suggest that back in 2020, Bustillos wrote about the e-book systems dominating libraries and schools. In one example, instead of just buying a book, a school had to pay $27 per student per year for continued access to copies of “The Diary of Anne Frank.”.

This is symptomatic of a broader system that treats true ownership of e-books and other digital media as a thing of the past. Instead, we “license” these e-books from their publishers, and they can be altered or removed at any time.

Sources indicate that “E-books are books,” Bustillos said. “They’re not some other thing. They are books, and people should be able to own them, and libraries should be able to own them, and media should be able to be owned. All digital media should be able to be owned.”.

In her view, ownership boils down to a simple question: “If you are at the mercy of somebody who can shut the book off, you do not own it.”.

So even beyond the question of ongoing payments, there have also been examples of e-books being altered or removed from readers’ devices long after their purchase. Bustillos acknowledged that for individual pieces of media, this distinction may not seem like a big deal, “but if it’s all the textbooks for everybody, if it’s all the books,” then it’s a real problem.

Sources indicate that flaming Hydra and The Phoenix Project seek to solve this by letting libraries truly purchase and own e-books. They can then lend those e-books to their patrons through a new, open source “library in a box” system called Lenny for Libraries.

In a recent development, the Phoenix Project is starting by offering five new e-books from Flaming Hydra writers, including collections of writing from The Awl, and of essays by Tom Scocca and Bustillos herself. That might sound like a relatively small start, but Bustillos said she’s talking to library consortiums and author groups, and the goal here is to “change the conversation” around e-books and digital archiving and lending. So The Phoenix Project could be paving the way for other initiatives that follow a similar model.

Similarly, The Phoenix Foundry Archive is designed to make paywalled newsletter content available to libraries. Bustillos noted that “so much of the best journalism, criticism, essays” is now being published in paywalled newsletters that are inaccessible to libraries (as well as the Internet Archive).

Flaming Hydra has been working on all this even before launching the Kickstarter, and Bustillos said she was grateful for the financial support from backers like Anand Raganathan, Brewster Kahle, and Paul Ford. But by turning to crowdfunding, Bustillos said Flaming Hydra can better protect the work, ensuring that it remains sustainable and independent.

In a recent development, “We don’t have to be at the mercy of anybody, and it also protects editorial independence,” she said. “Those things go hand in hand.”.

Flaming Hydra seeks to raise $30,000 for The Phoenix Project, with the campaign ending on November 27.

#40. Microsoft AI’s MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google and ElevenLabs on price and speed

Microsoft AI’s MAI-Transcribe-2 undercuts OpenAI, Google and ElevenLabs on price and speed

📅 03 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4742 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Venturebeat

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the company indicates is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs currently sells.
  • In a recent development, microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the firm claims is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs right now sells.
  • Recent findings suggest that that figure deserves a pause.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Microsoft AI on Thursday released MAI-Transcribe-2, a speech-recognition model the company indicates is faster, more accurate, and cheaper than anything OpenAI, Google, or ElevenLabs currently sells. Then it priced the thing at 10 cents per hour of audio.That figure deserves a pause. When Microsoft AI shipped the first model in this line just five months ago, it charged $0.36 an hour. Thursday's early-bird price cuts that by roughly 72%. For an enterprise processing 100,000 hours of call-center audio a year — a modest volume for a large bank or telecom — the bill drops from $36,000 to $10,000. At that level, transcription stops being a line item anyone argues about.The release arrives as Microsoft executes a strategy that would have seemed implausible two years ago: building its own frontier-class models one modality at a time, then steadily swapping them into products that once ran on OpenAI's technology. Transcription is the modality where that strategy has moved fastest, and MAI-Transcribe-2 is its clearest proof point yet. It also offers a preview of how the world's most valuable software company intends to compete in AI without depending on the partner it spent $13 billion to cultivate.What MAI-Transcribe-2 does and why the feature list matters to enterprise buyersThe model transcribes audio in 60 languages, up from 43 in June's MAI-Transcribe-1.5 and 25 in April's original release. It runs on Microsoft Foundry, the company's model marketplace for developers, and in MAI Playground, its testing environment. Microsoft says it built the model for the messy audio that real businesses generate — background noise, low-quality recordings, overlapping speech — rather than clean studio conditions.More important than the language count is what Microsoft has bundled into the base product. Speaker diarization sorts out who remarked what in a multi-person recording, which is the difference between a wall of text and a usable meeting transcript. Word-level timestamps attach a precise time marker to every word, enabling search, editing, and alignment with video. Keyword biasing lets developers feed the model a list of drug names, product codes, or employee names so it stops mangling domain jargon. Automatic language identification means users no longer have to declare the language in advance.Two features stand out for their specificity. A configurable output style offers a "verbatim" mode that preserves every "um," false start, and stutter for compliance and legal teams, alongside a "clean" mode that strips fillers for readable captions and notes. And code switching handles conversations that drift between languages mid-sentence; Microsoft explicitly names Hinglish and Spanglish, a nod to the Indian and U.S. Hispanic markets where a single customer-service call might toggle languages a dozen times. Specialty vendors have historically charged premiums for each of these capabilities. Microsoft is including all of them for a dime.How to read Microsoft's FLEURS and Artificial Analysis benchmark claimsMicrosoft makes three performance claims, each resting on a different measuring stick, and technical buyers should understand what each one captures and what it misses.The first is that MAI-Transcribe-2 ranks number one on FLEURS across 60 languages with an average word error rate of 5.2%. FLEURS is a benchmark Google researchers published in 2022, built from native speakers reading roughly 2,000 sentences in each of 102 languages — about 12 hours of speech per language. It is the standard yardstick for multilingual speech recognition because it lets you compare a model's Swahili against its Swedish on identical content. Word error rate, its metric, simply counts substitutions, insertions, and deletions against a human reference; 5.2% means roughly one word in 20 is wrong. But FLEURS is read speech, not conversation, and Microsoft's average has actually risen from the 3.7% it reported for MAI-Transcribe-1.5 in June. That almost certainly reflects broader coverage rather than regression — averaging across 60 languages instead of 43 means folding in low-resource languages where every model struggles — but buyers should request the per-language breakdown.The second claim is that the model ranks second on the Artificial Analysis word-error-rate leaderboard and defines that firm's accuracy-latency Pareto frontier. Artificial Analysis is an independent benchmarker that tests models through their public APIs, measuring what a customer actually gets. Its index blends simulated agent conversations, European Parliament speeches, and corporate earnings calls, weighting heavily toward English business speech. In June, the firm ranked MAI-Transcribe-1.5 third at 2.4% WER, behind Alibaba's Fun-Realtime-ASR-preview and ElevenLabs' Scribe v2, while calling it the fastest model in the top 10. Climbing to second suggests Microsoft has cleared ElevenLabs. "Pareto frontier" is the phrase practitioners should note: it means no rival beats the model on accuracy without being slower, and none beats it on speed without being less accurate.The third claim is raw speed — 10 times faster than OpenAI's GPT-Transcribe, seven times faster than ElevenLabs' Scribe v2, five times faster than Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, per Artificial Analysis evaluations. In batch transcription, speed matters less because anyone is waiting and more because throughput is cost. A model running at 300 times real-time needs a fraction of the GPU-hours of one running at 30 times. That efficiency is what lets Microsoft charge a dime and, presumably, still make money.Three speech models in five months: inside Microsoft AI's rapid release cadenceThe pace is the story within the story. On April 2, MAI-Transcribe-1 debuted with 25 languages at $0.36 per hour. On June 2, MAI-Transcribe-1.5 arrived with 43 languages, keyword biasing, and a third-place ranking on Artificial Analysis. Today, MAI-Transcribe-2 shipped with 60 languages, diarization, timestamps, code switching, a second-place ranking, and a price of $0.10.Three releases in five months, each expanding language coverage by roughly 40% while adding features competitors gate behind premium tiers. That cadence is characteristic of a team that has settled on a stable architecture and is now turning the crank on data and scale — the phase where speech models tend to improve promptly and predictably. It is also the cadence of a company that intends to make transcription a commodity before anyone else can.The organizational bet behind that speed is one Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI's chief executive, described to The Verge in April. He credited the first model to "a small, focused 10-person team" that had been "liberated from any of the bureaucracy," with a larger surrounding group handling vendor management and data acquisition.He also told The Verge the model ran at "half the GPU cost of the other state-of-the-art models," calling it "a huge cost-saving" for Microsoft. Meta, Amazon, Google, and Anthropic have all experimented with similar flattened structures, The Verge noted. Microsoft's transcription line is the most visible test yet of whether the approach produces commercial results rather than research papers.Why Microsoft is building its own AI models despite its $13 billion OpenAI betMicrosoft has invested more than $13 billion in OpenAI, and hosts OpenAI's models across Azure, Office, and Copilot. For most of the past four years, the obvious question about any Microsoft-built model has been: why bother? The answer has sharpened over the past year, and it begins with independence.When Microsoft hired Suleyman from Inflection AI in March 2024, along with most of Inflection's staff, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff read it as a declaration of intent. "Microsoft is building their own AI and I don't think Microsoft will use OpenAI in the future. They'll have their own frontier models," Benioff told CNBC in January 2025. "That's why they hired Mustafa Suleyman." Benioff had his own motives — Salesforce competes with Microsoft and invests in Anthropic — but events have largely borne him out.In October 2025, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership in a deal that, per Microsoft's own announcement, allowed Microsoft to "independently pursue AGI alone or in partnership with third parties" for the first time. Suleyman told The Verge that renegotiation "unlocked [Microsoft's] ability to pursue superintelligence," and Microsoft revealed its MAI Superintelligence team weeks later. In April 2026, the companies amended the deal again, ending Microsoft's exclusive access to OpenAI's models and eliminating Microsoft's revenue-share payments, according to reports at the time. Each amendment loosened the tie. Each one was followed by more MAI models.How Microsoft's in-house models are cutting costs across Teams, Word, and ExcelThe second half of the answer is margin. Every prompt Microsoft routes to an OpenAI model carries a cost. Every prompt it routes to its own model on its own GPUs carries a smaller one. In July, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had begun using MAI models to answer a portion of user prompts in Word and Excel — products it had previously advertised as powered by OpenAI and Anthropic. TechCrunch framed the shift as part of a broader industry pullback on AI spending, with Amazon, Uber, Meta, and Accenture all reportedly trimming.Transcription is the natural first target for this substitution because the problem is bounded and the metric is objective. Microsoft owns Teams, which generates an enormous volume of meeting audio. It owns Nuance, whose clinical documentation business runs on speech recognition. It owns the Azure speech services that thousands of enterprises already call. Every one of those workloads is a candidate to move onto MAI-Transcribe-2, and every hour that moves is an hour Microsoft no longer pays anyone else for.Suleyman has been unusually candid that this is the point. Superintelligence, he told The Verge in April, "is really about, 'Are these models capable of delivering product value for the millions of enterprises that depend on us to deliver world-class language models?'" Whatever one thinks of applying the word "superintelligence" to a transcription API, the commercial logic is plain: build the capability once, deploy it across a dozen products, and stop writing checks to a partner that is increasingly a competitor.MAI-Transcribe-2 vs. OpenAI, Google, and ElevenLabs: the competitive pictureMicrosoft's release names four rivals: OpenAI's GPT-Transcribe, Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, OpenAI's older Whisper V3-Large, and ElevenLabs' Scribe v2. It does not mention Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Speechmatics, or Rev — the specialists that have sold transcription to enterprises for a decade. Microsoft is positioning against the frontier labs, not the incumbents.That framing is partly marketing and partly true. The frontier labs have treated speech as a checkbox feature of broader platforms, priced accordingly, and a dedicated model that beats them on speed by five to 10 times while matching their accuracy is a genuine differentiator. But the specialists will feel the price pressure most acutely. At $0.10 an hour, Microsoft is pricing at or below where many of them sell high-volume enterprise contracts, and it is bundling diarization, timestamps, and 60 languages into the base rate. The specialists' remaining moat is domain depth — medical vocabularies, legal formatting, industry-specific integrations — and Microsoft's keyword biasing feature is aimed squarely at it.The one competitor Microsoft conspicuously does not claim to beat on accuracy is Alibaba, whose models have posted leading numbers on independent leaderboards for much of 2026. TechCrunch reported in July that some U.S. companies had begun evaluating Chinese models as cheaper alternatives despite security concerns. Microsoft's pitch to those buyers is implicit but unmistakable: comparable accuracy, faster inference, lower price, and a vendor your compliance team already trusts.The questions technical decision makers should ask before switching transcription vendorsFor all its specificity on benchmarks, the release leaves several practical questions open. The first is duration: Microsoft calls $0.10 per hour a launch offer without naming an end date or a standard rate, and anyone building a cost model should get both in writing. The second is streaming. The release emphasizes batch throughput and long-form audio but says nothing about real-time transcription, which voice agents and live captioning require. Artificial Analysis maintains a separate streaming leaderboard, and Microsoft's silence on it is notable.The third is per-language accuracy. A 5.2% average across 60 languages could mean 3% on major languages and 12% on low-resource ones, so buyers with specific needs should test those languages directly. The fourth is diarization quality. Word error rate does not measure speaker attribution; a transcript can have near-perfect WER and still assign every other sentence to the wrong person. The release offers no diarization error rate or comparable metric.The fifth is data handling. Enterprise transcription touches medical records, legal privilege, and financial disclosures, and the release says nothing about data residency, retention, or whether audio submitted to Foundry feeds future training. Microsoft's April announcements described training data as a mix of human-curated recordings, contractor-recorded noisy audio, and "vast amounts of data from the open web," per The Verge — a description that should prompt pointed questions from regulated industries. None of these gaps is unusual for a launch announcement, but they are exactly the questions that separate a leaderboard win from a production deployment.What Microsoft's speech model strategy reveals about its broader AI ambitionsStep back from the speech-recognition details and a pattern emerges that extends well beyond transcription. Microsoft's AI unit now ships models for images, voice, transcription, code, reasoning, and cybersecurity. At Build in June, it announced seven upcoming MAI models in a singlekeynote. Each follows the same playbook: target a well-defined modality, optimize aggressively for inference cost, price below the frontier labs, distribute through Foundry, and quietly swap the model into Microsoft's own products.This is not an attempt to build one model that beats GPT or Gemini at everything. It is an attempt to build a portfolio of specialized models that, in aggregate, let Microsoft serve most of its enterprise workloads without paying anyone else — and to sell the surplus capacity to everyone else at prices the specialists cannot match. Transcription happened to be the first modality where the approach fully matured, but the release notes for MAI-Transcribe-2 read less like a product announcement than a template.Suleyman has spent two years talking about "humanist superintelligence" and AI assistants that are "accountable to them, on their side." The vocabulary is lofty. The execution is a spreadsheet. Five months ago, Microsoft charged 36 cents to turn an hour of speech into text. On Thursday it charged a dime, threw in six features its rivals sell separately, and claimed the top spot on the industry's standard multilingual benchmark. The company that spent $13 billion learning what frontier AI costs has decided it would rather own the factory than rent the output — and now it is selling the output for less than the rent.MAI-Transcribe-2 is available now through Microsoft Foundry and MAI Playground.

Three releases in five months, each expanding language coverage by roughly 40% while adding features competitors gate behind premium tiers. That cadence is characteristic of a team that has settled on a stable architecture and is now turning the crank on data and scale — the phase where speech models tend to improve quickly and predictably. It is also the cadence of a organization that intends to make transcription a commodity before anyone else can.

The organizational bet behind that speed is one Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI's chief executive, described to The Verge in April. He credited the first model to "a small, focused 10-person team" that had been "liberated from any of the bureaucracy," with a larger surrounding group handling vendor management and data acquisition.

He also told The Verge the model ran at "half the GPU cost of the other state-of-the-art models," calling it "a huge cost-saving" for Microsoft. Meta, Amazon, Google, and Anthropic have all experimented with similar flattened structures, The Verge noted. Microsoft's transcription line is the most visible test yet of whether the approach produces commercial results rather than research papers.

Recent findings suggest that microsoft has invested more than $13 billion in OpenAI, and hosts OpenAI's models across Azure, Office, and Copilot. For most of the past four years, the obvious question about any Microsoft-built model has been: why bother? The answer has sharpened over the past year, and it begins with independence.

Industry observers note that when Microsoft hired Suleyman from Inflection AI in March 2024, along with most of Inflection's staff, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff read it as a declaration of intent. "Microsoft is building their own AI and I don't think Microsoft will use OpenAI in the future. They'll have their own frontier models," Benioff told CNBC in January 2025. "That's why they hired Mustafa Suleyman." Benioff had his own motives — Salesforce competes with Microsoft and invests in Anthropic — but events have largely borne him out.

In October 2025, Microsoft and OpenAI restructured their partnership in a deal that, per Microsoft's own announcement, allowed Microsoft to "independently pursue AGI alone or in partnership with third parties" for the first time. Suleyman told The Verge that renegotiation "unlocked [Microsoft's] ability to pursue superintelligence," and Microsoft announced its MAI Superintelligence team weeks later. In April 2026, the companies amended the deal again, ending Microsoft's exclusive access to OpenAI's models and eliminating Microsoft's revenue-share payments, according to reports at the time. Each amendment loosened the tie. Each one was followed by more MAI models.

Industry observers note that the second half of the answer is margin. Every prompt Microsoft routes to an OpenAI model carries a cost. Every prompt it routes to its own model on its own GPUs carries a smaller one. In July, Bloomberg reported that Microsoft had begun using MAI models to answer a portion of user prompts in Word and Excel — products it had previously advertised as powered by OpenAI and Anthropic. TechCrunch framed the shift as part of a broader industry pullback on AI spending, with Amazon, Uber, Meta, and Accenture all reportedly trimming.

Sources indicate that transcription is the natural first target for this substitution because the problem is bounded and the metric is objective. Microsoft owns Teams, which generates an enormous volume of meeting audio. It owns Nuance, whose clinical documentation business runs on speech recognition. It owns the Azure speech services that thousands of enterprises already call. Every one of those workloads is a candidate to move onto MAI-Transcribe-2, and every hour that moves is an hour Microsoft no longer pays anyone else for.

In a recent development, suleyman has been unusually candid that this is the point. Superintelligence, he told The Verge in April, "is really about, 'Are these models capable of delivering product value for the millions of enterprises that depend on us to deliver world-class language models?'" Whatever one thinks of applying the word "superintelligence" to a transcription API, the commercial logic is plain: build the capability once, deploy it across a dozen products, and stop writing checks to a partner that is increasingly a competitor.

Microsoft's release names four rivals: OpenAI's GPT-Transcribe, Google's Gemini 3.5 Transcribe, OpenAI's older Whisper V3-Large, and ElevenLabs' Scribe v2. It does not mention Deepgram, AssemblyAI, Speechmatics, or Rev — the specialists that have sold transcription to enterprises for a decade. Microsoft is positioning against the frontier labs, not the incumbents.

That framing is partly marketing and partly true. The frontier labs have treated speech as a checkbox feature of broader platforms, priced accordingly, and a dedicated model that beats them on speed by five to 10 times while matching their accuracy is a genuine differentiator. But the specialists will feel the price pressure most acutely. At $0.10 an hour, Microsoft is pricing at or below where many of them sell high-volume enterprise contracts, and it is bundling diarization, timestamps, and 60 languages into the base rate. The specialists' remaining moat is domain depth — medical vocabularies, legal formatting, industry-specific integrations — and Microsoft's keyword biasing feature is aimed squarely at it.

Sources indicate that the one competitor Microsoft conspicuously does not claim to beat on accuracy is Alibaba, whose models have posted leading numbers on independent leaderboards for much of 2026. TechCrunch reported in July that some U.S. companies had begun evaluating Chinese models as cheaper alternatives despite security concerns. Microsoft's pitch to those buyers is implicit but unmistakable: comparable accuracy, faster inference, lower price, and a vendor your compliance team already trusts.

For all its specificity on benchmarks, the release leaves several practical questions open. The first is duration: Microsoft calls $0.10 per hour a launch offer without naming an end date or a standard rate, and anyone building a cost model should get both in writing. The second is streaming. The release emphasizes batch throughput and long-form audio but says nothing about real-time transcription, which voice agents and live captioning require. Artificial Analysis maintains a separate streaming leaderboard, and Microsoft's silence on it is notable.

According to recent reports, the third is per-language accuracy. A 5.2% average across 60 languages could mean 3% on major languages and 12% on low-resource ones, so buyers with specific needs should test those languages directly. The fourth is diarization quality. Word error rate does not measure speaker attribution; a transcript can have near-perfect WER and still assign every other sentence to the wrong person. The release offers no diarization error rate or comparable metric.

The fifth is data handling. Enterprise transcription touches medical records, legal privilege, and financial disclosures, and the release indicates nothing about data residency, retention, or whether audio submitted to Foundry feeds future training. Microsoft's April announcements described training data as a mix of human-curated recordings, contractor-recorded noisy audio, and "vast amounts of data from the open web," per The Verge — a description that should prompt pointed questions from regulated industries. None of these gaps is unusual for a launch announcement, but they are exactly the questions that separate a leaderboard win from a production deployment.

According to recent reports, step back from the speech-recognition details and a pattern emerges that extends well beyond transcription. Microsoft's AI unit now ships models for images, voice, transcription, code, reasoning, and cybersecurity. At Build in June, it declared seven new MAI models in a singlekeynote. Each follows the same playbook: target a well-defined modality, optimize aggressively for inference cost, price below the frontier labs, distribute through Foundry, and quietly swap the model into Microsoft's own products.

This is not an attempt to build one model that beats GPT or Gemini at everything. It is an attempt to build a portfolio of specialized models that, in aggregate, let Microsoft serve most of its enterprise workloads without paying anyone else — and to sell the surplus capacity to everyone else at prices the specialists cannot match. Transcription happened to be the first modality where the approach fully matured, but the release notes for MAI-Transcribe-2 read less like a product announcement than a template.

It has been revealed that suleyman has spent two years talking about "humanist superintelligence" and AI assistants that are "accountable to them, on their side." The vocabulary is lofty. The execution is a spreadsheet. Five months ago, Microsoft charged 36 cents to turn an hour of speech into text. On Thursday it charged a dime, threw in six features its rivals sell separately, and claimed the top spot on the industry's standard multilingual benchmark. The manufacturer that spent $13 billion learning what frontier AI costs has decided it would rather own the factory than rent the output — and now it is selling the output for less than the rent.

MAI-Transcribe-2 is available now through Microsoft Foundry and MAI Playground.

#39. The pros and cons of using cloud storage over local storage

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (616 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Engadget ↗ Open Full Page

The pros and cons of using cloud storage over local storage

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (616 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cloud storage can be super convenient, but there are times when using local storage is the better move.
  • Recent findings suggest that external hard drives and USB flash drives are usually easy ways to back up your files, especially since they don't require an internet connection or waiting for uploads.
  • It has been revealed that your photos, videos, contacts and more are all synced to the cloud without having to copy each file manually.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cloud storage can be super convenient, but there are times when using local storage is the better move.

Recent findings suggest that external hard drives and USB flash drives are usually easy ways to back up your files, especially since they don't require an internet connection or waiting for uploads. You just plug them into your computer, copy the files you need, and that's it. But cloud services like iCloud and Google Drive have also made it a lot easier to back up everything — and most of the time, it all happens automatically.

It has been revealed that your photos, videos, contacts and more are all synced to the cloud without having to copy each file manually. Plus, there's no risk of leaving your external drive somewhere or damaging it to the point where you lose your files. That doesn't mean cloud storage is perfect, and both have their pros and cons — it really comes down to choosing what works best for your needs. If you're unsure whether to choose local or cloud storage to back up your data, here's how the two stack up on access, cost and reliability.

In a recent development, sharing files through a cloud service is also much easier than sharing them from local storage. Once a file is uploaded to the cloud, you can easily share it with someone with just a click  — cloud platforms generate a link so others can view and download that file. There's also collaboration, so multiple people can work on the same document or spreadsheet at the same time. Platforms like Google Docs even offer tools that allow each collaborator to leave comments in real time, perfect for workplaces and schools.

Safety is another big plus, since major cloud providers keep copies of your data spread across multiple servers and data centers. The chances of something bad happening and you losing all your data are very low – though not impossible. Plus, your cloud account can be protected with a password and two-factor authentication, meaning others can't just take your files from you.

Sources indicate that cloud storage relies on a stable internet connection, and you're prone to unexpected outages. A slow connection or an outage on your provider's servers could prevent you from downloading a file when you need it most. Also, uploading and downloading large files can take a while if you're using a slow connection. With an external SSD, you can copy gigabytes of files in just minutes. Internet has no impact on local storage, so it's something to consider if you're always traveling and rely on mobile data, for example.

It has been revealed that cost is another reason that might push people away from cloud services. While you only have to pay once to buy an external hard drive, cloud providers typically charge recurring subscription fees on a monthly or annual basis. Apple charges $9.99 per month in the US for 2TB of iCloud+, which comes to nearly $240 if you pay for two years — and the storage isn't really yours. Stop paying, and your files may be deleted after a while, not to mention possible price increases down the road. By comparison, you can find 2TB SSDs for around $290, but they'll always be yours, with no extra charges.

That doesn't mean you should ditch the cloud and rely entirely on local storage. Subscribing to a cloud service that allows you to back up all your files and access them from anywhere is very handy, and you can also benefit from local storage by offloading some of your larger files or those you really want to make sure you never lose.

#38. Logitech Yeti 2 Review: An All-In-One Studio Setup

📅 15 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1515 w)
