💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.
  • Meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.
  • "Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat. "Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.There is substance behind both parts of that claim. Muse Spark 1.3 makes significant gains over last month’s 1.2 release, particularly on long-running agent tasks. The version developers can access now is also one of the strongest price-performance offerings near the top of independent model rankings.Meta’s strongest Muse Spark 1.3 benchmark results come from its max reasoning configuration. Meta notes that version is still completing additional safety testing and will arrive “shortly”; the third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says it evaluated max in a limited partner preview, and currently lists no API provider at all for the configuration. The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh.That makes the more relevant enterprise question not whether Muse Spark 1.3 can reach frontier territory, but how close the model companies can actually deploy today gets — and at what real cost.The shipping model is very good, but not the benchmark leaderMeta does disclose results for both configurations in its underlying evaluation report, so this is not a case of the firm hiding the deployable model. But its launch materials prominently showcase the max variant, and some of the largest scores belong to that configuration.For example, Meta reports GDPval-AA v2 scores of 1,754 Elo for max versus 1,709 for xhigh, OSWorld 2.0 scores of 66.9 versus 57.2, and JobBench scores of 64.9 versus 61.2. On some tests the distinction is negligible or reversed: DeepSearchQA is tied at 89.4, while xhigh scores 89.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus max at 88.8.Artificial Analysis scores Muse Spark 1.3 max at 62 on its Intelligence Index and the shipping xhigh version at 61. The latter ties GPT-5.6 Sol max, Grok 4.6 high and Claude Opus 5 high. But Anthropic still occupies the top of the leaderboard: Claude Fable 5.1 reaches 66 at max and 65 at xhigh, while Claude Opus 5 reaches 63 at max and xhigh.In other words, Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh is legitimately in the frontier cluster, but it is not the model currently setting the frontier.That is still a substantial change from Muse Spark 1.2. VentureBeat’s coverage of last month’s launch found Meta fielding a credible coding challenger that nevertheless generally trailed Anthropic’s best model. Muse Spark 1.2 scored 82.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus Opus 5’s 86.7%, and also finished behind Opus on the other main coding comparisons Meta presented.With 1.3, Meta is no longer merely showing up in that contest. On several coding and agentic evaluations, it is trading wins with OpenAI and Anthropic.Meta says the underlying model has also become easier to operate. Muse Spark 1.3 is trained to maintain multiple workflows in a long thread, gather context with tools, detect gaps in its own plans, ask users for clarification when necessary and confirm before consequential actions. In Meta engineers’ internal comparisons, it used roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than 1.2 during coding work.For enterprises paying for thousands or millions of agent loops, those behavioral improvements could matter more than another leaderboard point.‘Almost too cheap to meter’ does not mean Meta cut its pricesMuse Spark 1.3 did not receive an API price cut. Meta kept Standard pricing exactly where it was for Muse Spark 1.2: $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens and $0.15 per million cached input tokens.ModelInput ($/1M)Output ($/1M)Total ($/1M)SourceMuse Spark 1.2 / 1.3 Contributor$0.10$0.20$0.30MetaMiMo-V2.5 Flash$0.10$0.30$0.40XiaomiDeepSeek-V4-Flash — off-peak$0.22$0.66$0.88DeepSeekGPT-5.6 Luna$0.20$1.20$1.40OpenAIMiniMax-M3$0.30$1.20$1.50MiniMaxLongCat-2.0 — limited-time promo$0.30$1.20$1.50LongCatDeepSeek-V4-Flash — peak hours$0.44$1.32$1.76DeepSeekMiMo-V2.5$0.40$2.00$2.40XiaomiDeepSeek-V4-Pro — off-peak$0.66$1.98$2.64DeepSeekLongCat-2.0 — standard$0.75$2.95$3.70LongCatMiMo-V2.5 Pro (≤256K)$1.00$3.00$4.00XiaomiGemini 3.7 Flash — through Dec. 31, 2026$0.75$3.75$4.50GoogleGemini 3.8 Flash — through Dec. 31, 2026$0.75$3.75$4.50GoogleDeepSeek-V4-Pro — peak hours$1.32$3.96$5.28DeepSeekMuse Spark 1.1 / 1.2 / 1.3$1.25$4.25$5.50MetaGLM-5.3$1.40$4.40$5.80Z.AIGrok 4.6 — <200K prompt tokens$2.00$6.00$8.00xAIMiMo-V2.5 Pro (>256K)$2.00$6.00$8.00XiaomiQwen3.8-Max$2.00$6.00$8.00QwenCloudGemini 3.7 Flash — starting Jan. 1, 2027$1.50$7.50$9.00GoogleGemini 3.8 Flash — starting Jan. 1, 2027$1.50$7.50$9.00GoogleGPT-5.6 Terra$2.00$12.00$14.00OpenAIGrok 4.6 — ≥200K prompt tokens$4.00$12.00$16.00xAIGPT-5.4$2.50$15.00$17.50OpenAIKimi K3$3.00$15.00$18.00Moonshot AIClaude Opus 5$5.00$25.00$30.00AnthropicSakana Fugu Ultra (≤272K)$5.00$30.00$35.00Sakana AIGPT-5.6 Sol — Standard mode$5.00$30.00$35.00OpenAIClaude Fable 5 / Claude Mythos 5$10.00$50.00$60.00AnthropicClaude Fable 5.1 / Claude Mythos 5.1$10.00$50.00$60.00AnthropicGPT-5.6 Sol — Fast mode$10.00$60.00$70.00OpenAIThat makes Zuckerberg’s “almost too cheap to meter” line less a statement about lower token prices than about what Meta believes developers can accomplish with those tokens.Artificial Analysis offers evidence for that argument, but also a complication. It measures Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh at 235.2 output tokens per second and estimates a cost of $0.55 per Intelligence Index task. At 61 on the Intelligence Index, that gives it the lowest cost per task of any currently measured model at that intelligence level. Muse Spark 1.2 cost only $0.40 per Artificial Analysis task, while scoring 57. Despite unchanged per-token pricing, the independent benchmark’s cost of completing an average task therefore increased generation-over-generation. Artificial Analysis attributes the increase primarily to heavier input-token consumption on agentic evaluations. That does not directly contradict Meta’s claim of 25% lower token use: Meta is describing comparisons in its own coding workflows, while Artificial Analysis is measuring a broader suite of reasoning and agentic tasks. But it illustrates why “cheap” becomes slippery once models operate as agents. Token rates, reasoning effort, number of turns, tool calls and retries all contribute to the actual cost of finishing work.Meta also retains its unusually cheap Contributor tier — $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.20 per million output tokens — in exchange for permission to use prompts and completions for training. As VentureBeat noted with Muse Spark 1.2, that may be attractive for prototyping but creates a materially different data-governance calculation for enterprises working with proprietary code or sensitive internal information.Wang’s ‘Gemini who?’ lands on an unusually close comparisonMeta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang was considerably less qualified in celebrating the release.After Artificial Analysis posted its Muse Spark results, Wang reposted them on X, adding: “i really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 😱💨”The shade was particularly pointed because Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on the same day, pitching it at almost exactly the same class of workload: long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents and multi-step professional reasoning. Google calls 3.8 its best reasoning and coding Flash model yet and says it is the company’s third Flash release in six weeks. Independent numbers give Wang something to work with, though hardly a knockout.Artificial Analysis gives Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh a 61 Intelligence Index score at $0.55 per task, compared with 59 and $0.58 for Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning. Meta therefore edges Google on both intelligence and task cost at those particular settings. Google wins decisively on throughput. Artificial Analysis measures Gemini 3.8 Flash high at about 305 output tokens per second, versus 235 for Muse Spark — roughly 30% faster. Gemini also has the lower raw API sticker price for now: Google is charging an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, compared with Meta’s $1.25 and $4.25.That promotional Google pricing expires December 31, after which it rises to $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. Meta’s newest AI model Muse Spark 1.3, unveiled yesterday, is faster and more performant on third-party benchmarks than its predecessor — with a caveat.

"Muse Spark 1.3 is rolling out today with frontier performance almost too cheap to meter," Meta co-founder and CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote on X, calling it Meta’s “biggest jump” yet in coding and agentic work.

There is substance behind both parts of that claim. Muse Spark 1.3 makes significant gains over last month’s 1.2 release, particularly on long-running agent tasks. The version developers can access now is also one of the strongest price-performance offerings near the top of independent model rankings.

Meta’s strongest Muse Spark 1.3 benchmark results come from its max reasoning configuration. Meta says that version is still completing additional safety testing and will arrive “shortly”; the third-party benchmarking firm Artificial Analysis says it evaluated max in a limited partner preview, and right now lists no API provider at all for the configuration.

The version broadly rolling out this week through its Muse Code harness and the Meta Model API uses Meta’s previously available reasoning settings, including xhigh.

That makes the more relevant enterprise question not whether Muse Spark 1.3 can reach frontier territory, but how close the model companies can actually deploy today gets — and at what real cost.

Meta does disclose results for both configurations in its underlying evaluation report, so this is not a case of the company hiding the deployable model. But its launch materials prominently showcase the max variant, and some of the largest scores belong to that configuration.

For example, Meta reports GDPval-AA v2 scores of 1,754 Elo for max versus 1,709 for xhigh, OSWorld 2.0 scores of 66.9 versus 57.2, and JobBench scores of 64.9 versus 61.2.

On some tests the distinction is negligible or reversed: DeepSearchQA is tied at 89.4, while xhigh scores 89.2 on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus max at 88.8.

Recent findings suggest that artificial Analysis scores Muse Spark 1.3 max at 62 on its Intelligence Index and the shipping xhigh version at 61. The latter ties GPT-5.6 Sol max, Grok 4.6 high and Claude Opus 5 high. But Anthropic still occupies the top of the leaderboard: Claude Fable 5.1 reaches 66 at max and 65 at xhigh, while Claude Opus 5 reaches 63 at max and xhigh.

In other words, Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh is legitimately in the frontier cluster, but it is not the model currently setting the frontier.

That is still a substantial change from Muse Spark 1.2. VentureBeat’s coverage of last month’s launch found Meta fielding a credible coding challenger that nevertheless generally trailed Anthropic’s best model. Muse Spark 1.2 scored 82.9% on Terminal-Bench 2.1 versus Opus 5’s 86.7%, and also finished behind Opus on the other main coding comparisons Meta presented.

Recent findings suggest that with 1.3, Meta is no longer merely showing up in that contest. On several coding and agentic evaluations, it is trading wins with OpenAI and Anthropic.

Meta notes the underlying model has also become easier to operate. Muse Spark 1.3 is trained to maintain multiple workflows in a long thread, gather context with tools, detect gaps in its own prepares, ask users for clarification when necessary and confirm before consequential actions. In Meta engineers’ internal comparisons, it used roughly 20% fewer tool calls and 25% fewer tokens than 1.2 during coding work.

For enterprises paying for thousands or millions of agent loops, those behavioral improvements could matter more than another leaderboard point.

Muse Spark 1.3 did not receive an API price cut. Meta kept Standard pricing exactly where it was for Muse Spark 1.2: $1.25 per million input tokens, $4.25 per million output tokens and $0.15 per million cached input tokens.

That makes Zuckerberg’s “almost too cheap to meter” line less a statement about lower token prices than about what Meta believes developers can accomplish with those tokens.

Artificial Analysis offers evidence for that argument, but also a complication. It measures Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh at 235.2 output tokens per second and estimates a cost of $0.55 per Intelligence Index task.

At 61 on the Intelligence Index, that gives it the lowest cost per task of any presently measured model at that intelligence level.

Muse Spark 1.2 cost only $0.40 per Artificial Analysis task, while scoring 57.

Industry observers note that despite unchanged per-token pricing, the independent benchmark’s cost of completing an average task therefore increased generation-over-generation. Artificial Analysis attributes the increase primarily to heavier input-token consumption on agentic evaluations.

That does not directly contradict Meta’s claim of 25% lower token use: Meta is describing comparisons in its own coding workflows, while Artificial Analysis is measuring a broader suite of reasoning and agentic tasks.

Recent findings suggest that but it illustrates why “cheap” becomes slippery once models operate as agents. Token rates, reasoning effort, number of turns, tool calls and retries all contribute to the actual cost of finishing work.

Meta also retains its unusually cheap Contributor tier — $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.20 per million output tokens — in exchange for permission to use prompts and completions for training.

As VentureBeat noted with Muse Spark 1.2, that may be attractive for prototyping but creates a materially different data-governance calculation for enterprises working with proprietary code or sensitive internal information.

Meta chief AI officer Alexandr Wang was considerably less qualified in celebrating the release.

According to recent reports, after Artificial Analysis posted its Muse Spark results, Wang reposted them on X, adding: “i really hate to say it, but… gemini who? 😱💨”.

Sources indicate that the shade was particularly pointed because Google released Gemini 3.8 Flash on the same day, pitching it at almost exactly the same class of workload: long-horizon software engineering, autonomous agents and multi-step professional reasoning. Google calls 3.8 its best reasoning and coding Flash model yet and states it is the organization’s third Flash release in six weeks.

Independent numbers give Wang something to work with, though hardly a knockout.

Artificial Analysis gives Muse Spark 1.3 xhigh a 61 Intelligence Index score at $0.55 per task, compared with 59 and $0.58 for Gemini 3.8 Flash at high reasoning. Meta therefore edges Google on both intelligence and task cost at those particular settings.

In a recent development, google wins decisively on throughput. Artificial Analysis measures Gemini 3.8 Flash high at about 305 output tokens per second, versus 235 for Muse Spark — roughly 30% faster. Gemini also has the lower raw API sticker price for now: Google is charging an introductory $0.75 per million input tokens and $3.75 per million output tokens, compared with Meta’s $1.25 and $4.25.

That promotional Google pricing expires December 31, after which it rises to $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens.

Industry observers note that the result is a useful snapshot of how tight frontier-model economics have become. Meta presently wins this independent comparison by two Intelligence Index points and three cents per benchmark task; Google offers substantially higher output throughput and cheaper raw tokens during its launch promotion.

Wang’s “gemini who?” is fun executive trash talk. For an enterprise architect, the answer is closer to: Gemini is the faster option; Muse is currently the slightly stronger high-effort agent by this independent measure.

The more consequential matter for some developers may have little to do with today’s benchmark race.

When Meta debuted Muse Code and Muse Spark 1.2 in August, VentureBeat noted how dramatically the firm had moved away from the open-weight strategy that made Llama ubiquitous.

Muse Code and Spark 1.2 were proprietary, API-served products — a striking posture for the manufacturer that had spent years arguing that open AI was the path forward.

Five days later, Meta changed course again.

It has been revealed that on August 10, it released the 30-billion-parameter Muse Glimmer under an Apache 2.0 license. Zuckerberg also mentioned: “In the coming weeks, we are also going to open the weights for Muse Spark 1.2.” Reuters separately reported Meta’s plan to release the Spark 1.2 weights.

Now, Meta has instead shipped Muse Spark 1.3 as another proprietary model.

That does not yet amount to a broken promise — “coming weeks” can reasonably describe a period longer than three weeks. But today’s announcement makes the roadmap less clear rather than more.

Recent findings suggest that meta’s new post no longer notes Muse Spark 1.2. It says its roadmap includes “the Muse Spark open weights release”, without identifying a version, release date, model size or license. Zuckerberg likewise said on X that “Muse Spark open weights releases” are coming soon.

For teams that standardized on Llama because downloadable weights meant self-hosting, customization and control over inference economics, that ambiguity may matter more than whether Spark gained another point on a composite benchmark.

It has been revealed that muse Spark 1.3 reveals that Meta can now iterate proprietary frontier models at extraordinary speed. The shipping xhigh configuration is fast, competitively priced and much closer to the top of independent rankings than its predecessors. The max preview shows Meta can push the family a little further when allowed to spend more reasoning compute.

The next test is different: whether Meta can convert that pace into a roadmap enterprises can actually blueprint around — including making its best capabilities broadly deployable and delivering the open-weight Spark model it has already noted is coming.

The oldest gadget in your house could be your home network's biggest security hole

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Your home network is only as secure as its weakest link.
  • In a recent development, it may not seem like you would need to replace a perfectly functional 10-year-old connected camera in your home.
  • Many of us don't realize how often gadgets need to be replaced, and it's not just cameras.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Your home network is only as secure as its weakest link.

In a recent development, it may not seem like you would need to replace a perfectly functional 10-year-old connected camera in your home. However, your network is only as secure as its weakest link, and that's often a device that is so outdated it no longer receives updates from its manufacturer.

Many of us don't realize how often gadgets need to be replaced, and it's not just cameras. Security cameras should be replaced every five to seven years, with router manufacturer Netgear recommending a hardware replacement every four or five years. You'll know it's well beyond time to replace your router when you start experiencing slower connections. At that point, you may already be facing security concerns.

When outdated gadgets like these are compromised, they could be sending your data to bad actors or working as part of a botnet. In 2025, the FBI issued a warning that end-of-life (EOL) routers–devices that are no longer receiving software updates or security patches–are being compromised by cybercriminals. It's ultimately up to the consumer to perform a regular device audit to determine if routers, cameras and other smart devices pose a security risk.

Recent findings suggest that any connected device in your home that no longer receives bug patches and security updates may be a risk. Per a 2024 Consumer Reports study, most appliance makers don't tell consumers in advance how long they will offer updates to software. It found that of 19 major brands that make smart appliances, only three told customers how long they would maintain support, and even the longest promised about five years of updates, falling short of consumer expectations of 10.

Routers are also often at risk. A 2025 FBI warning stated that routers dated 2010 or earlier likely no longer receive updates and should be replaced. In this particular case, such gadgets were being targeted by malware called TheMoon, which infects routers to install proxies, so criminals can operate anonymously. TheMoon hack doesn't even require a password, instead exploiting open ports and a vulnerable script. Even if you have a strong password, an old router can be a risk.

Industry observers note that routers and other smart devices that have been hacked can be recruited as part of a botnet, a network of devices used to overwhelm websites with traffic to take them offline. A recent report from Cisco found that nearly 40 percent of the vulnerabilities attackers targeted most affected end-of-life devices, and about a third of exploited vulnerabilities were at least a decade old. The report focused on businesses, but the lesson applies at home too: Attackers keep targeting old hardware because it never gets fixed. Even if most of your cameras and routers are up to date, just one outdated device can allow bad actors to enter the network and compromise anything else connected to it.

Industry observers note that the latest standard for router security is WPA3. To upgrade your router from WPA2, go to the router's admin page, find the wireless security setting and choose WPA3. Some older gadgets will struggle to connect after switching, so choose WPA2/WPA3 if you run into that problem. If there is no WPA3 option, it is time to replace the router.

According to recent reports, to make your home network more secure in general, turn off remote management and use a strong password. Never use the default password that came with your router. Turn on automatic updates to ensure firmware is updated as soon as it is offered. Otherwise, you can put any old gadgets and smart appliances on a separate network so that, if they are compromised, they can't get to more crucial gadgets like your laptop or phone. It's worth noting, though, that the data stored on outdated gadgets is still vulnerable, so it's always best to replace old hardware for maximum security.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent on Sunday called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after CEO Jensen Huang's resignation, questioning whether the chipmaker pursued illicit sales of its advanced artificial intelligence chips to boost earnings.

According to recent reports, bessent remarked Nvidia's board should look outside the tech giant for its next chief executive and suggested other executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with U.S. export controls.

"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent noted in an interview on Fox News.

The remarks come amid a growing feud between Bessent and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick over the suspected diversion of advanced AI chips to China, even as the Treasury secretary continues to defend President Donald Trump's handling of the matter.

Both Bessent and Lutnick are expected to accompany Trump to China this week, Semafor reported Sunday, putting the two Cabinet secretaries alongside the president as he prepares to meet with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin on the sidelines of the APEC summit.

A White House official told Reuters on Thursday that the president maintains "complete confidence" in Lutnick, despite mounting scrutiny of the secretary’s handling of the Nvidia matter.

In a recent development, huang resigned Thursday following revelations about his relationship with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of spying for China. Megaspeed is suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export controls.

Nvidia named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim CEO.

Bessent suggested Sunday that Nvidia's problems extended well beyond Huang.

"If this were a bank and they hadn't complied like this, the OCC would be in there right now, and a lot of the executives would be removed," Bessent mentioned, referring to the Office of the Comptroller of the Currency.

Bessent also questioned Nvidia's financial disclosures, pointing to a surge in reported Singapore revenue as its China sales fell.

Nvidia stopped separately reporting Singapore revenue in November 2025, saying a upcoming methodology based on customers' headquarters rather than billing addresses better reflected the geographic distribution of its sales.

Bessent's remarks came two days after he told CNBC's "Squawk Box" that several federal agencies had supported adding Megaspeed to the government's export blacklist for months.

"But Commerce has the pen," Bessent said.

The public rebuke followed reporting by Axios that Bessent confronted Lutnick in the White House Situation Room over Commerce's failure to act against Megaspeed. Commerce denied that the confrontation took place.

According to recent reports, lutnick is also facing scrutiny over his family's financial ties to Nvidia. CNBC reported Friday that Cantor Fitzgerald, the Wall Street firm formerly run by Lutnick and now led by his sons, has helped arrange billions of dollars in financing for Nvidia's business partners.

It has been revealed that cantor remarked Nvidia share holdings fell nearly 50% over six months as national security concerns surrounding Huang escalated. The positions were associated with client swap transactions, not proprietary investments, the investment bank said.

There is no evidence Lutnick shared sensitive information with his sons or that Cantor traded on such information.

Bessent on Sunday said Trump had drawn a firm line against sales of chips more advanced than Nvidia's H200 to China. Trump himself authorized H200 sales to approved Chinese customers in December —following months of lobbying by Huang — in an arrangement under which the U.S. government would receive a 25% cut.

Bessent's latest criticism comes two days before Nvidia is scheduled to report its first quarterly earnings since Huang's departure.

How the world’s fires changed while humanity hit pause

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1435 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ars Technica

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives.
  • In a recent development, many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts.
  • Industry observers note that A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wildfires occur worldwide, and they can sometimes become serious threats to people’s lives. A series of massive bushfires from 2019 to 2020 swept across southeastern Australia and destroyed thousands of homes. Recently, the 2025 Los Angeles wildfires spread widely across the city, resulting in massive damage to local communities.

In a recent development, many things can cause wildfires, but humans are the only factor that can also make preventative efforts. Measuring people’s impact on fire is difficult because of the mix of human and natural influences.

Industry observers note that A team led by Jianghao Wang, a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences, recently published a study in Cell Reports Sustainability comparing the COVID-19 era with other years. Data from the 2020 lockdowns suggest that lower human activity at this time had the net effect of lowering average fire activity.

Fire doesn’t just happen anywhere. Although plenty of flammable materials exist in natural settings, not every place experiences wildfires. Some prairies burn almost every year, while many forests go without major fires for hundreds of years. Researchers explain these differences in terms of fire regimes, which are patterns describing when, how often, and how widely and intensely fires occur.

In a recent development, weather is a major factor affecting fire regimes. An abundance of rain helps grow grass and trees that can become fuel for fires. Whether they do or not, however, can depend on the moisture inside plants; plants with enough moisture do not burn easily. By contrast, dry conditions make them more likely to catch fire. When a drought lasts, vegetation becomes increasingly flammable. Strong winds also accelerate fire growth and spread enormously.

Industry observers note that human activity often combines with weather conditions to cause fires. Even routine outdoor recreation can accidentally start a fire. More people venture outdoors during sunny, drier times of the year, increasing the risk of accidental fires when dry vegetation is more likely to be present.

Sources indicate that the double-sided role of humans in fire also adds to the difficulty. Humans do start fires, but they also put them out. Firefighters contain fires that could have gone worse if no action had been taken and can keep them from spreading. Humans can also take preventative actions, such as clearing flammable material.

It has been revealed that sometimes the line between starting fires and preventing them becomes blurred. One way to clear out flammable material is to intentionally set fires to make future fires more manageable. However, these fires are hard to distinguish from other fires through satellite monitoring.

An experiment is one way to find out how humans affect wildfires. If everyone stayed home under the same weather, their impact on fires would be revealed. This is why Wang’s research team focused on the COVID-19 era. It was what’s called a “natural experiment,” in which experimental conditions arose without any action by researchers.

Wang explained: “Human activity and climate normally vary together, because seasons, farming calendars, and weather all shape both fire and human behavior. The early-2020 lockdowns produced an abrupt, large-scale drop in human mobility, and the timing differed across countries while the weather did not change in the same way. This gave us a natural experiment.”.

The researchers defined the period of restricted mobility by checking regional lockdown orders and mobile phone location data. Data from NASA and the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration’s Suomi NPP satellite helped the team track fires. Its VIIRS sensor detects heat signatures from fires at a spatial resolution of 375 meters. Each hot spot the satellite detects counts as an active-fire detection, meaning one large fire can appear as multiple spots. However, the satellite records both wildfires and prescribed burns without distinguishing between them. As a result, the intent behind each fire remains unknown.

In the study, detections during the 2020 restriction periods were compared with those from the same weeks in 2013–2019. Weather conditions weren’t exactly the same as in past years, which was accounted for.

Sources indicate that the results show that areas under lockdown in the first half of 2020 had about 12.3 percent fewer active-fire detections than the recent-past average. The drop varied by vegetation type. In forests, fires decreased by about 27.7 percent, while grasslands decreased by 8.4 percent. Shrublands, savannas, and croplands didn’t show much difference. The researchers interpret this to mean that humans are a major cause of fires in forests and grasslands.

Industry observers note that controlling for weather factors was notable in the study. Without adjustments, the drop was only 5.8 percent, which was not statistically significant. After controlling for weather, however, the estimated decline increased to 12.3 percent. If weather in 2020 were more favorable to fires than in previous years, it might have masked some of the human impact.

In a recent development, the 12.3 percent decrease in fire detections doesn’t mean that humans directly caused this share of fires. Restricting human activity shrank both humans’ impact on starting fires and likely limited their impact on extinguishing them. The 12.3 percent figure is the net effect after these two opposing forces partly cancel out.

Wang remarked, “The 12.3 percent is a net effect, not the share of fires caused by humans; opposing changes in ignition and suppression mean it does not capture the full magnitude of human influence.”.

In regional data, some areas experienced a considerable increase in fire after human mobility was restricted. Most of South America, southern Africa, and northeast Asia saw an increase in fire during the COVID-19 lockdowns. Notable increases include 31.4 percent in Colombia, 25.4 percent in India, and 70.7 percent in Honduras.

According to recent reports, there are no direct field data showing why this occurred. The researchers inferred that diminished fire suppression capacity resulted in more fires in these locations, but Wang acknowledged, “It is an inference, not a direct observation.” That inference was based in part on earlier studies that suggested that weaker fire management in Colombia and Madagascar contributed to increased fires.

In a recent development, one line of evidence is how fires reacted to different levels of mobility loss, based on fire counts in 0.5-degree grid cells. In countries with fewer fires, fire declined in almost a straight line as mobility decreased. But countries that experienced more fires demonstrated a slow increase that leveled off at about 27 percent on average as mobility fell. The researchers interpreted this as a sign that different mechanisms were at work. The steady decline fits fewer human-driven ignitions, while the gradual rise points to weakened suppression. But Wang mentioned that there could be other reasons, such as changes in local land use.

Recent findings suggest that mobility restrictions may also have disrupted fire management activities, which could mean that fewer fires were set for management purposes. The researchers examined 12 countries with records of prescribed burning. The area burned by prescribed fires in 2020 decreased by about half compared to the 2013–2019 average. Of course, the locations and sizes of prescribed burns also shift from year to year with fire return intervals and land-management cycles, which complicates this analysis.

When areas subjected to prescribed burning were excluded in those 12 countries, the decline in fires there shrank from 45.3 percent to 27.8 percent.

This research has limits partly because it relied on mobile phone data to track human movement. This kind of data might not capture human activity in rural areas where coverage may be limited. Also, the analysis focused only on the first half of each year, so the impact on regions where fires happen more frequently in the latter half of the year, such as the western US, may not have been fully captured.

Wang explained that this quasi-experimental design provides strong associational evidence but is not a controlled experiment.

Industry observers note that wang emphasized that the study is not an evaluation of fire policies. The analysis does, however, suggest that there’s no single ideal policy response. Where fires decreased, human ignition seems to dominate. In those areas, reducing accidental ignitions through public education and maintaining beneficial prescribed burning can be important. On the other hand, areas where fires increased might need to address reduced monitoring and suppression. Maintaining firefighting and patrol capacity during disruptions can be important there.

Wang added, “Overall, a uniform policy is unlikely to work, and strategies should be tailored to local human-fire relationships.” Fire-risk projections might benefit from accounting for human behavior. That way, more accurate fire projections can be made even as weather and society change.

A Chinese state-linked hacking group compromised executive laptops at an agricultural industry conference on Hainan Island this spring — not through phishing or a network breach, but by breaking into hotel rooms and booting the machines from a USB stick while the executives were at dinner. CrowdStrike, which tracks the group as OVERCAST PANDA, disclosed the campaign in its 2026 Threat Hunting Report and detailed the operation's timeline in an interview with VentureBeat at Fal.Con 2026: an intruder entered one room at around 8 p.m. local time and a second room by 9:57 p.m., writing a backdoor called FlowCloud directly to each laptop's storage before rebooting the machines and leaving. There was no network intrusion, no phishing email, and no credential stolen through a login page.The report dates the intrusions to between March and May 2026, and the timestamps come from Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike's senior vice president of counter adversary operations, who cleared them for publication in the VentureBeat interview. CrowdStrike's OverWatch team disrupted the intrusions and assessed that OVERCAST PANDA will almost certainly continue. Physical-access operations are rare across the 290 named adversaries CrowdStrike tracks, according to Meyers, and MUSTANG PANDA's version depends on a dropped USB stick the victim plugs in. What Meyers identified as novel is the combination of hotel-room entry by a state intelligence service with malware deployment, booting the target machine from the USB rather than relying on a user to execute a file from it.When the executives powered on the next morning, the trigger fired and FlowCloud loaded. Keylogging, screen capture, file collection, and credential harvesting began."We have the visibility once the machine boots up," Meyers told VentureBeat. A registry key or similar trigger starts FlowCloud sometime after the operating system loads, and that's when Falcon's sensor picks it up. The gap is the window between the USB write and the next boot — the hours the laptop sits compromised and undetected before the executive logs back in.CrowdStrike published that gap a month before it announced its AI security product slate — Falcon Guardian, SafeMind, the Agentic Identity Provider, and AI Gateway — at Fal.Con 2026 this week.Why existing security tools missed itEDR needs the operating system loaded and the agent running. MFA waits for a login attempt, phishing training for an email, AI agent security for an agent to secure.OVERCAST PANDA bypassed all of them at the point of entry. The initial compromise completed below the running OS, below the EDR agent, below the authentication stack. Falcon caught FlowCloud once its process started after boot, but by then the implant and its trigger were already on disk."Hotel entry is a very common thing," Meyers remarked. "Talk to any corporate physical security person. They're generally aware of hotel entry, but I think what is unique is the combination of hotel entry with deployment of malware."Meyers said he thinks China's Ministry of State Security sits behind OVERCAST PANDA. The people entering the rooms are either officers or agents of the MSS or the Ministry of Public Security, or hotel housekeeping staff the services have bribed or compelled, Meyers told VentureBeat. A separate mid-2026 intrusion targeted a U.S.-based media professional using the same tradecraft, according to the report. The ability to audit security-related BIOS settings on the laptops executives carry has sat inside the platform for seven years. Pointing it at travel devices is a decision, not a product gap.The controls that would have blunted the OVERCAST PANDA campaign are old and cheap, and each does a different job. Disabling external boot in UEFI removes the vector. A BIOS administrator password keeps it disabled. He used temporary laptops and email accounts on overseas trips while at CrowdStrike, wiping the device when he returned. The exposure starts at customs. "You can't intrude on physical devices at scale. And even then, it's just one device." The person in the room is the target, and the intrusion rarely pivots further, he added. Falcon Guardian ships to one team, and BIOS configuration on travel laptops belongs to another. The Agentic IdP rolls out under identity governance while the decision about whether executives carry production-access machines to international conferences sits with a different group. And the budget line that funds cloud-threat defense has nothing to do with travel-device policies.Meyers has lived both sides. "I've talked to companies where they're like, we're having a board meeting in Shanghai, and I'm like, why would you do that?"What security leaders need to do before the next tripAudit every executive laptop for USB boot status. If the device can be booted from USB right now, it has the same gap OVERCAST PANDA exploited this spring. The steps below cover Windows laptops, the platform FlowCloud targets.Enforce full-disk encryption with pre-boot authentication. BitLocker in a TPM-only configuration is a documented weak point against physical access. SCRT researchers pulled the volume master key off the LPC bus with a $49 FPGA module in 2021, and Dolos Group did the same over SPI that year. OVERCAST PANDA wrote a backdoor and its post-boot trigger to the Windows volume, so the operators had write access to it. That points to machines that were either unencrypted or protected by a configuration the operators defeated. Pre-boot authentication with a PIN or USB key forces a human step before storage becomes readable.Verify Secure Boot is enabled and the revocation list is current. Secure Boot validates signatures on boot components and blocks most unauthorized bootloaders, but it leaves external media bootable and signed shims can still carry a bypass. ESET published findings on 11 legacy Microsoft-signed UEFI shims in July 2026 that let untrusted code run at boot on any machine trusting Microsoft's third-party certificate. Microsoft revoked them in its June 9, 2026 DBX revision, so a laptop that skipped that update still trusts them. Lock the boot order at the UEFI level, disable one-time boot menus, and set a BIOS administrator password that covers both the setup utility and any boot-override key. Meyers' read is that a lot of these settings go unchecked because the fix is inconvenient.Issue travel-only devices for international conferences with no access to production systems, no saved credentials for internal tools, and no persistent VPN configuration."If they can get their hands on it, they can own it," Meyers put it, citing an old DEF CON adage. Falcon catches FlowCloud only after boot — the exposure is the hours between the USB write and the next login, while the laptop sits closed and compromised."It's cheap to buy a couple of laptops and a couple of phones," Meyers said. The controls that close that window are a handful of firmware settings and a spare laptop. The question is whether anyone has deployed them.

#16. How to clear the application cache on your Mac

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (602 w)

How to clear the application cache on your Mac

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (602 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Engadget

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Clearing app caches don’t necessarily make your Mac run faster.
  • Recent findings suggest that your Mac applications often store temporary files, called caches, to improve user experience.
  • Industry observers note that for example, Google Chrome builds its app cache as you visit different websites.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Clearing app caches don’t necessarily make your Mac run faster.

Recent findings suggest that your Mac applications often store temporary files, called caches, to improve user experience. This is a recommended best practice that most developers follow to prevent apps from creating or redownloading the same files each time you use them. App caches include temporary files like image previews, downloaded content and other data that help apps launch rapidly and serve content without additional processing.

Industry observers note that for example, Google Chrome builds its app cache as you visit different websites. It caches parts of webpages, like images, which helps speed up load times when you visit the same website next time. However, the problem with leaving application caches unchecked is that it could continue taking up storage space even when an application no longer requires the cached files.

Although your Mac may manage these temporary files, there's no guarantee when this process occurs. Moreover, problematic app caches can contribute to glitches, like displaying outdated or inaccurate content. Knowing how to clear app caches on your Mac can help resolve complications arising from an outdated cache or reclaim storage space wasted on bloating caches.

Some Mac applications allow clearing app caches from within the app itself. For example, Safari and Apple Music include the options to clear app caches in their settings menu. However, this is not the case for every Mac app out there; you'll need to manually find their caches to delete them.

Your Mac typically stores application caches in ~/library/caches. Since the library is treated as a hidden directory, your Mac may not readily reveal it in the Finder. To view the library folder: Finder > command + shift + H > command + J > check "show Library Folder." Once in the library folder, press command + J > check "Calculate all sizes" to display folder sizes alongside folder names.

Recent findings suggest that in the caches folder, look for the application cache you want to clear. You can distinguish third-party apps from first-party Apple apps from the folder names and prefixes. First-party Apple apps use the "com.apple" prefix in their bundle identifier, while third-party apps don't. Open the application folder in question and delete everything inside to clear its app cache. If an app cache doesn't exist in the caches folder, you can look for it in ~/library/containers. The containers folder includes apps that run in a sandbox, so their cache is also isolated. Whether your app caches are in caches or containers, you'll need to apply the same principle for finding and deleting them.

It's worth understanding that clearing app caches doesn't necessarily improve application performance unless your Mac is already running short on storage space. However, deleting app caches can help reclaim storage space and sometimes even resolve app glitches. When you launch an app after clearing its cache, you might notice the app taking longer to launch, and using it might feel sluggish. This happens because the app has to rebuild its cache all over again. However, once this process is complete, your app should feel smooth and snappy to use.

In a recent development, it is not recommended to indiscriminately clear app caches or build a maintenance routine that involves one. Your Mac apps rely on caches to ensure a smooth user experience. You should only ever clear app caches if you notice the app not behaving as expected or if an app is taking up too much storage space. Otherwise, it's best to leave app caches alone and let your Mac manage it at its discretion.

Pixel Tag is a brilliant Band-Aid on a Find Hub network Google can’t easily fix

📅 15 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (821 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5google

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good.
  • In a recent development, the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software.
  • Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Google Pixel Tag is here and, at least so far, it’s really good. But fresh hardware and some new features can’t fix the core problem. Google’s Find Hub network has been restricted from the very start, and it’s not something Google can easily fix.

In a recent development, the good news on Pixel Tag: this is a well-built tracker that, unlike others, is the clear product of the hardware having direct access to the software. Little touches like being able to adjust ringer volume on the fly combine nicely with UWB – the latter something we rarely see on third-party devices largely due to Apple – all things that elevate the Find Hub tracker to what we called the latest “gold standard.”.

The bad news: this is still a Find Hub tracker.

Google’s Find Hub network has improved dramatically over the two years since its launch. Where Google originally had to admit that tracking performance was lacking (a nice way of putting it, frankly), improvements started arriving in 2025. We noticed that the network seemed to be working much better a few months after its wide rollout, and Google later confirmed speed improvements.

But, ultimately, the Find Hub network is still reeling from how it debuted.

Google had a privacy focus when launching what was originally called the “Find My Device” network, defaulting the network to only be active on Android phones in “high-traffic areas” only. Users could switch this to “all areas,” but the initial rollout defaulted to effectively cutting off anywhere that wasn’t a major metro, airport/travel hub, etc. It left the network useless to many. Google defended this as a “first-of-its-kind safety protection,” but I’d argue it hindered the network into a state of inefficacy.

Recent findings suggest that again, it’s gotten better since then, but it’s still not as good as it should be. Samsung’s network, limited solely to Galaxy phones, shouldn’t outperform Google’s. Find Hub trackers should be just as good as AirTags and the third-party trackers that work with Apple’s network. They’re just not, and I truly do believe it all boils down to this initial choice. One of the reasons this is getting better is that Google has been pushing users to the “all areas” setting during the setup of a fresh device – I’ve noticed this on some recent devices I set up, but it’s not been completely consistent just yet. That’s a good step forward but, even if it is the new default, that still requires millions of users to upgrade their devices, and we’ve never been in a better time to not upgrade your phone.

Sources indicate that all of that is to say, the Pixel Tag isn’t fixing this problem. Surely, it’ll give Google some needed fire to fix the problem, but new hardware isn’t the solution. That’s something I was discussing with 9to5Google readers on our review. UWB is a tentpole feature of the Pixel Tag, but it doesn’t change the network problems, it just improves precision finding. We needed a first-party tracker like this regardless of the state of the network, something that really takes advantage of the platform and pushes it forward, but it’s just a quick fix, a Band-Aid.

What do you think? Have you found the Find Hub network reliable enough, or is there still room for improvement? Sound off in the comments below!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that iPhone Duo has been out for about 3 weeks now, and I’ve happily been using mine since launch day. Many people have made a big deal about the app situation, but I’d largely say most apps I rely on are updated for iOS 27.0 at least.

That mentioned, a fair number of apps are still from iOS 26 and earlier, and those apps have letterboxing. In my time since trying the phone, I feel one quick adjustment could make the letterboxing a lot less of an matter.

Recent findings suggest that right now, on the home screen, iPhone Duo allows you to long press an app and open it in Split View. All iPhone Duo apps allow Split View, even if the developer hasn’t compiled it for iOS 27 or 27.1.

It has been revealed that one of the beautiful things about iPhone Duo Split View is the fact that you don’t have to decide what you’re splitting right away. On the other half of the display, you’ll see your home screen, and you can later decide what app to open.

Industry observers note that so, given the fact that a non iOS 27 app will only occupy around half of the inner display anyways, I feel like it’d make sense to have an option to open every non-optimized app in Split View by default – rather than needing to select it every time. Or, better yet, toggle certain apps to always open in Split View.

Certain apps, even if they’re optimized for iOS 27, don’t quite feel right spread across the wider inner display of iPhone Duo – so it’d be nice to always have them in a half split without needing to think about it.

This would be a small UX improvement that I feel would go a long way, so if Apple could implement this on iPhone Duo – it’d certainly help out the app situation. While they’re at it, it’d be nice to have Slide Over on the iPhone Duo, for when you want to promptly see a smaller app on top of your full screen app.

#13. The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

The 4 Best Planners of 2027: Roterunner, Hobonichi, Cloth & Paper

📅 03 Jan 2024 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3737 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that there’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027.
  • According to recent reports, the world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand.
  • In a recent development, after years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that there’s nothing like the feeling of a brand-new planner, and I've found the best planners if you're shopping for something new for 2027. Whether you're looking to get a little more organized or just love having somewhere to write everything down, the beginning of the year is a great time for a fresh start, and most planner companies have their 2027 planner designs already available.

According to recent reports, the world of planners might seem simple if you've only browsed your local Target or bookstore to see what planners they might have on hand. But there's a wide world of options out there that can perfectly suit your needs, especially if you're willing to build your own travel notebook or write in the dates on an undated paper planner, or open to trying your first Japanese-style planner.

In a recent development, after years of testing and a constant stack of planners on my desk, I've found these standout favorite planner styles that could benefit everyone. If you're looking for a tech companion to your paper planner, check out my guides to the Best Digital Wall Calendars and Best Digital Notebooks to help keep your calendar and thoughts organized digitally.

Updated November 2026: I've updated the information in this guide to reflect planner availability as 2026 comes to an end and 2027 designs become available. I'm also currently testing 2027 designs from Plum Paper, Laurel Denise, My PA Planner, and Sterling Ink, plus an undated design of Aura Estelle if you're looking for a planner you can start using in December 2026 into the new year.

If you need a single planner that can do it all and won't burn through your back-to-school budget, this is the one. The Roterunner Purpose Planner is an undated planner that has monthly spreads, weekly spreads, and two full open pages for each week, so there's plenty of room to write longer lists or a project brainstorm. Each monthly and weekly spread has a ton of premade checklist sections for you to use, too. There's even space to track your meals, water intake, and gratitude. It's a planner that actually helps me stay organized and gives me space to track and take notes without running out of room.

Sources indicate that the undated nature makes it easy to pick up anytime and use for whichever months you need. Fell off the boat for a few months? No problem. No pages will go to waste when you can fill them in as you go. It only covers six months, but I actually like that; it once again feels like a feasible commitment, especially if you're waffling on how much paper planner you want to promise to use. I love the massive B5 size ($35) since it's finally enough space for me and all my various to-do lists and brainstorms, but there's also a smaller (and cheaper!) A5 ($28) size. It's truly my go-to planner since it has so much space for me to both use the pre-made lists and the open space to actually stay organized and put all my ideas, plans, and notes into one planner. Most others make me feel like I need a companion notebook, but not the Roterunner.

The covers come in a variety of simple colors, and in both hard cover or soft, but the butter-soft faux leather soft cover is my favorite of the bunch. Get it in B5 size if you're always looking for more room in your journals and planners—you won't regret it.

Amazon (Techo, January 2027 Start).

Amazon (Cousin, January 2027 Start).

In a recent development, if you're getting into planners, there's no way you won't hear about Hobonichi at some point. There are a few different planners the brand makes, with the Techo being the most popular model. I tested the similar Hobonichi Cousin, which adds weekly spreads to the front of the planner after the monthly overviews. While I don't typically prefer a daily planner style, I was surprised by how much I liked using the Hobonichi. All of Hobonichi's planners use Tomoe River S paper, which is super thin but won't bleed through to the other side. It's also super smooth to the touch and to write on. I liked adding my own structure to the daily pages; I sketched a box to separate my to-do lists and habit trackers from my hourly agenda for the day, and then would usually freeform the rest of the page based on what was on my mind. The Cousin I tested and photographed is an A5 size, while the standard Techo is the smaller A6.

According to recent reports, hobonichi's 2027 editions are here, so you can stock up on your planner for next year right now, plus tons of colors, covers, and other accessories, some of which are unique to 2027. I recommend picking out a protective cover since I did ding up my soft cover quite a bit, and that was just from being used around the house with an occasional trip in a bag. There are little quotes in the corners, but I got a Japanese version instead of an English one, so I can't actually read mine. But honestly, I'm glad I did; I prefer the Japanese lettering to English words on the corners of each page.

Shop (Single Notebook, A5 Slim).

Shop (Clear Vinyl Cover, A5 Slim).

Shop (Travel Notebook Set, A5 Alim).

Industry observers note that I've been obsessed with travel notebooks this year. A travel notebook uses bands to connect three or four notebooks together, and I love using this system to build a customized planner designed for my exact needs. It makes it easy to change the design, too, since you can just switch out a single notebook when it's full.

According to recent reports, I really like Cloth & Paper's Travel Notebook Collection. There are 13 different notebooks you can choose from to include in your travel notebook, ranging from classic weekly and monthly spreads to more unique options like a daily wellness notebook and a task planner. It's really a great option if you want a couple of specific things, or even just a regular monthly and weekly notebook plus a blank notebook in the back you can fill with to-do lists and replace anytime without needing an entirely new planner. It's great for students, too, because you can have a notebook dedicated to tracking your assignments and syllabus for the semester. You'll need to create your own, though, as Cloth & Paper doesn't have a dedicated academic notebook for you to select.

Recent findings suggest that I tried both the A5 Slim and the Pocket Plus size, and I really prefer the A5 Slim for a traditional planner experience. The Pocket Plus would be fun to bring on a trip; I wish I'd had it on my latest trip to store little mementos and key things like parking receipts, and could have also written out notes and the proposal for the week-long trip. But otherwise, the larger A5 slim was much easier to write on and use for my daily notes and planning.

You'll want the Clear Vinyl Travel Notebook Cover ($23 to $25) no matter which size you choose, which includes elastic bindings to bring all the notebooks you buy together, and you can also pick up more colorful elastic options to add a little more personality to your planner.

Erin Condren (Academic Planner).

I've heard a lot of good things about Erin Condren. Founded in 2005 by Erin Condren, it's known for the LifePlanner that's full of various spreads and productivity tools that you can customize, but there are other variations of planners you can find from the brand. While you'll usually customize your Erin Condren planner if you shop directly on the site, there's a predesigned Target line you can shop that won't give you options, but will give you a well-made planner that's ready to go immediately.

Industry observers note that I've been testing the Erin Condren Academic Planner you'll find at Target, but it's sold out as we head into the new year; Erin Condren's website has similar, but more expensive options with more cover and customization options. This base version from Target is a great fit for students and people with deadline-style or client-based work they want to organize. Each month has two pages following the monthly spread to set your most vital to-dos and dates, but also a full page to track the month's deadlines and what class (or client, or in my case, story beat) they're for. After that, there are weekly spreads with long columns for each day, and seven blocks of four lines that you can label with things like specific classes, clubs, or organizations, or parenting and household tasks, as I track. It's been a really easy planner to add into my lifestyle, even though it's made for students. There's a class tracker in the front of the planner, too, which I skipped using, plus a detailed holiday calendar, and the back has project and exam pages, plus blank note pages, and even a simple sheet of stickers with things like “Exam,” “Midterm,” and “Paper Due.”.

In a recent development, academic planners usually start in August, so you probably don't want a planner like this if you want something fresh for the new year. But it's still my favorite I've tried if it's your preferred style. Erin Condren does have annual layouts and its popular LifePlanner designs available in 2027 layouts, and other specific designs like budget planners and teacher lesson planners if you're looking for something specific, too.

Like I remarked, there's a huge world of planners out there. Here are a few that the Reviews team and I at WIRED have tested and enjoyed.

In a recent development, the Kokuyo Jibun Techo is another Japanese planner, but this one is a travel-notebook-style design, making it more customizable with a cover and multiple books that fit inside it. The First Kit comes with three books that fit into the included cover: Diary (labeled simply with the year), Life, and Idea. The 2026 versions are sold out, but you can buy the 2027 versions right now.

Looking for more of a monthly planner? The Significant A## Planner is a massive planner with a nice monthly spread you can literally spread across your desk, with plenty of writing space for each day. Best for working from home, though; you don't want to have to fit this into your work bag.

If you're looking for a great daily planner, the Day Designer is a popular option for a reason. It's bulky since it has pages for every single day, but it leaves room for both your schedule and a long to-do list.

Plum Paper (A5 Vertical Priorities).

Plum Paper is my favorite classic-style planner, and you can easily customize it to start at any time of year and design the pages to fit your needs. I especially like the weekly A5 Vertical Priorities layout, and you can add all kinds of customizations into the daily columns, the habit tracker, and more to make it exactly what you want. But I've also left the habit tracker blank so I can adjust my habits as needed all year long.

In a recent development, I bought this no-frills hardback during Prime Day last year, figuring I couldn’t go wrong for less than 20 bucks, and I was right. It’s a handy A5 size with a monthly view calendar at the beginning of each month, and then a 5-by-2.5-inch square for each day. That’s it. There are some plain lined pages in the back if you need more space for notes, but if your planning consists only of to-do lists and tracking deadlines, you will love this.—Kat Merck.

It has been revealed that agendio Basic Planner starting at $48: This is a completely customizable planner. I liked it, and you have the option to design your own pages, and the folder-style cover will protect both the pages and binding. I didn't love the customization tools or abilities as much as I wanted to, and there are a lot of steps to create your planner. I preferred the custom tools of Plum Paper over it. It's a good planner if the pages and binder-style are what you're looking for, and you can find some preset options that usually start around $48 for the smallest page size and black-and-white print.

Recent findings suggest that ban.do 12-Month Planner for $20: If you're looking for another affordable option but want something with more personality than the Roterunner above, Ban.do's planners are fun and colorful and even come with a page of stickers. It's only a horizontal weekly format, though, which I don't love (but maybe you do!) and the 2027 12-Month designs are now available.

According to recent reports, happy Planner 12-Month Planner for $33: Happy Planner uses disc-bound planners to make it easy to remove and add pages or covers, which is nice for customizability. But they're a very specific aesthetic, and personally, I didn't love turning pages on the discs. Still, it's a good planner if you like the style, and they come in a ton of different layouts. Right now, you can get a Happy Planner that starts in July 2026 and will run you until June 2027, perfect for tracking the academic year.

It has been revealed that laurel Denise Nancy Academic Planner for $44: These planners are cool because you'll look at the month and your weekly at the same time, as the slim weekly pages lay on top of the monthly spread. However, I write way, way too much for the space in these planners, at least for the Nancy design I tested previously. It's great if you just want to write a couple to-dos and meetings per day, but if you want space for detailed lists, you might feel the way I did. I'm presently testing the 2027 Luna ($62) and Scout ($62) planners from Laurel Denise to see if I still feel the same way compared to the original design.

Leuchtturm1917 12-Month Ruled Planner for $29: This is a solid, minimalist planner that has a popular following. It's a simple horizontal weekly layout with the week on one side and a lined page on the other. It's not enough space for everything I write down, but if you're looking for something simple and space for a couple of lists or notes for each week that fit onto a page, it's a good option for you. Leuchtturm1917 also has a nice line of notebooks that look the same from the outside cover, so make sure you actually get the planner.

It has been revealed that muji Undated Weekly Planner for $7: If you want a super simple, super affordable planner, the Muji Undated Weekly is for you. It's just undated weekly horizontal spreads from front to back, even on the paper cover. It's slim, but still more than a year's worth of weeks in it. It's the most minimalist planner I've tried, and though I'm not a fan of horizontal weekly spreads for my planner needs, it's a great cheap option for a lot of people.

Recent findings suggest that papier Hardcover 2027 Planner for $40: My favorite thing about Papier's planners is how gorgeous the covers are. Papier has a range of beautiful designs you can choose that feel like they belong on a bookshelf rather than just my planner. I tested one of the annual planners, which has the horizontal weekly layout I don't love on any planner (and you can still get that by choosing the mid-year layout for any cover Papier has if you love that style), but the academic one ($29) has a vertical layout that's much more up my alley. Whichever style you like, you can pick. Papier also has softcover academic planners ($32) that use a ring binding, which is easier to lay open than the hard cover binding, and still has both mid-year and academic layout options.

Passion Planner 2027 Planner for $50: This planner was really popular when I was in college, and maybe it still is with the college kids. I liked it, but I feel like the Purpose Planner does a similar thing but better, at least for my needs. It's got vertical spread, but every slot is timed, so I can't use it as a to-do list. It's great for anyone needing to strategy out a super detailed schedule and has some to-do list spaces on the bottom, but they're pretty small in my opinion to work for an entire week. It's good for students who only want to track their busy schedules and a couple assignments and tasks for each week.

Industry observers note that looking for what to pair with your planner? Here are some of our team's favorite daily tools and planner accessories.

It has been revealed that passion Planner Passion Highlighters for $20: If your planner could use a little color, I really like Passion Planner's highlighter sets. They're nice and thin-tipped to fit into slim planner lines, and I especially like the vintage colors for adding color without it feeling neon-bright. You can use the highlighters to organize your looks by type (I like to do red for work, blue for my kid, yellow for things like doctor's appointments, and green for my social life) or color-code your class subjects like we used to do with ringed notebooks.

Pilot Metropolitan Fountain Pen for $34: I never understood the appeal of a fountain pen until I bought one. A properly smoothed fountain pen nib requires very little pressure to write with and seems to glide across the page with a soft, satisfying scratching sound. I know, I'm one of those people now. Much of my initial skepticism came from the perceived complexity of caring for and using a fountain pen, which is very much overblown. My favorite pen of the dozen I've tested is the Pilot Metropolitan with the fine nib. It's easy to work with, taking either prefilled ink cartridges, which you can pop in and out without ever spilling any ink, or you can fill it yourself using a converter and the ink of your choice. I started off using the cartridges, but eventually my quest for a waterproof ink led me to the converter and this sketching ink. Once a week or so, I dip the Metropolitan nib in the bottle of ink and twist the converter to fill the chamber with ink—that's all there is to it. Whichever fountain pen you find works best for you, you’ll find you'll have a quite simply better writing experience. —Scott Gilbertson.

According to recent reports, plum Paper Seasonal Stickers for $10: There are a lot of stickers out there you could use for your planners, but my favorites—especially for the holidays—are from Plum Paper. They're beautiful and fun, and are mostly nice and small to fit into small lines or monthly charts without eating up the entire section. I like that there's a mix of shapes and styles, and you can also shop stickers for themes like home, fitness, wellness, and baby milestones. You can even make your own custom stickers (starting at $12), which are only thick line-style stickers where you can customize the word and icon on them. Still, very handy!

It has been revealed that not everyone needs or wants a rigid planner. If you just need daily to-do lists or are a fan of bullet journals, consider getting a great notebook instead.

Maybe you just want a plain, lined notebook. One of our former reviewers recommended the Midori MD Notebook, and I found it to be a nice small size if you're looking for something minimal. It comes in lined, unlined, or dot-grid, and uses paper made from cotton pulp (just like money!) Midori’s notebooks are designed to fit inside notebook or journal covers (which you can find all over Etsy). The pages are a subtle off-white and have a weight and texture that draw you in.

According to recent reports, one of our reviewers skips a planner entirely and instead writes down his to-do list on a 3-by-5 index card. He puts that index card into his pocket with a pocket-sized memo book like this one from Field Notes ($13 for three), where he jots down notes throughout the day to use for the next day's to-do list. Both the notebook and index cards fit inside a waxed canvas notebook cover to keep them safe from the elements (or just his pocket). It's an affordable and easy-to-manage system.

Studies show that it's good for your brain to write things down. Sure, you could put your calendar in an online tool, but putting pen to paper activates more brain connectivity. We're more likely to remember and learn things if we write them down by hand, so using a paper planner for your to-do list can make it easier to remember. Plus, it's fun! You're given a creative space to let out everything you need to remember, from appointments to the day's tasks, and customize it in a way that best helps you stay organized.

What Style Paper Planner Is Best for You?

According to recent reports, paper planners mainly come in two styles: weekly and daily. Daily planners have an entire page dedicated to each day, while weekly planners have an entire week spread across just two pages. These aren't the only options (monthly is another popular one, for example, but not as popular as these two styles), but they're the most common you'll see. I like daily planners for folks who have a really busy schedule they want to initiative out, and long daily to-do lists. Weekly planners are great if you want to be able to write down a few things per day but don't need an entire page.

What Sizes Do Planners Come In?

Recent findings suggest that here are a couple common planner sizes. My favorite are the larger sizes since I like lots of room to doodle, but the smaller A5 is a popular choice for a book-sized planner that won't take up too much space. Not all paper planners use the same sizing names—Moleskine, for example, calls its A5 size a large—so you'll want to check measurements before you purchase.
